A longstanding issue in graph neural networks lies in their limited extensibility and lack of a unified design theory. To address this challenge, we developed a comprehensive GNN framework called Universal Pyramidal Linear Transform and Rewiring (UPLTR), consisting of a modularized skeleton based on a universal pyramidal structure and incorporating two core ideas: hierarchical feature transformation with local structure reconfiguration. The proposed architecture, characterized by a Universal Pyramidal Structure (UPS) consisting of three primary components - the global set of nodes, the local set of nodes, and the edge set - and seamlessly integrating global and local features through two layers of linear transformation, as well as Local Structure Rewiring (LSR) which enables the adjustment of graph topology according to network requirements. Furthermore, we introduced the representation of node, local set and edge, and edge set, and graph learning of UPLTR, as well as the expansion of its application to various fields including image classification, community detection and network representation. The experimental results confirm the exceptional performance of UPLTR in these areas.

The need to complete partially observed matrices from real-world data sources has gained significant prominence in data analysis. In this context, we delve into low-rank matrix completion, a technique for filling in missing values in partially observed matrices by assuming they have a low rank. A major challenge arises when analyzing large datasets, as ensuring data privacy becomes a priority. To address this, we utilize the Huber framework to combine robustness and privacy, ultimately providing more accurate low-rank matrix completions. We demonstrate that choosing the huberization parameter, p, is key to achieving optimal results, and our findings suggest suitable p values for specific data types. Through experiments using synthetic and real-world data, we evaluate the performance of this new approach, comparing it to existing differential privacy methods.

The overall appearance of space (excluding stars) is defined by tiny particles, called dust. These tiny dust particles, typically measuring a few nanometers in size, contribute to the blocking of light in interstellar space and are responsible for the formation of new stars. Larger interstellar dust particles, ranging in size from 0.01 micrometers to 0.5 micrometers, exhibit unique optical properties that result from electron scattering and emission caused by the interaction of incoming interstellar radiation with these particles. A primary concern of many researchers is the uncertainty surrounding the precise effects of these dust particles on our understanding of the observed properties of galaxies. To achieve a more precise understanding, researchers rely on a variety of analytical tools, including polarized light observation, infrared emission analysis, and the use of various dust extinction models. Recent studies have integrated the effects of different types of dust particles (carbon grains, silicate grains, and larger interstellar dust particles) into a unified framework. This unified framework, called the astrodust+PAH framework, is then used to simulate the effects of these dust particles under real-world conditions. A key aspect of this unified framework is its ability to reconcile existing models, including the commonly used Rieke & Lebofsky model. This unified framework is then used to simulate and analyze different dust-related phenomena, including the interaction of light with dust particles, the emission of infrared light from dust particles, and the polarized light of galaxies. The specific details and impact of external factors that cause the precession and changes in gas disks surrounding low-mass stars are still largely unclear. This study focused on the PDS 30 system, consisting of a low-mass star and two massive planets, where our analysis of the HST/STIS data revealed further details about the orbit and extent of the precession in the disk surrounding the star. We found that the outer planet, PDS 30 d, at a distance of 30 au, is responsible for the observed precession rate of 22-28 days and may have created a void in the disk surrounding the star. We also observed a significant decrease in emission from the disk surrounding the star at wavelengths less than 1 microns resulting in an increase in the estimated mass loss rate, reaching 10^7 mo/y following the formation of the void. This increased rate in estimated mass loss is consistent with the predicted outcome resulting from the action of a massive planet in the disk surrounding the star.

The objective of the Lights Out problem is for a robot to reach a switch in as few steps as possible. However, the challenge presented here is a non-standard version where the robot's movements have consequences beyond just reaching the switch. Each time the robot clicks a light, it counts as a point, but if it turns off a light that was previously lit, it loses a point. This "maximum clicks" version of the Lights Out problem is explored alongside other non-standard variants where the robot starts with a set number of lights or specific lights that are already lit. By using the same search algorithm to find solutions, the complexity of these modified problems can be understood. Moreover, it has been determined that the minimum number of lights needed to make the "maximum clicks" challenge difficult enough to be unsolvable by simple algorithms is 9. Interestingly, it was also discovered that the "maximum clicks" challenge is solvable for all configurations with 8 or fewer lights, but it is unsolvable for certain configurations with 9 or more lights, and this result holds true for certain other configurations as well.

This paper presents a novel model for image division called the variational image partitioning model, along with its corresponding numerical algorithm. The model's core components are an image segmentation task, which involves dividing an image into distinct sections, and a process to restore these segments to clear and unified areas within the image. The newly developed model offers a straightforward approach to both segmentation and restoration, reducing the overall complexity. Through various visual demonstrations, it is shown that this model effectively tackles a range of visual challenges, even when other methods fail. Moreover, the model's effectiveness is further supported by experimental results showing its superiority in dealing with difficult cases compared to a range of standard approaches.

The fixed-point iteration used in Abstract Interpretation can be inefficient due to its necessity to iterate until convergence, which may not utilize computational properties of the chosen abstract domain. Depending on the domain's characteristics, altering the order of operations in the iteration loop can speed up computational processing. This presentation outlines a domain-independent procedure that separates the iterative process into ascendant and descendant phases. These phases can be further optimised by identifying and exploiting computational properties in the domain. This work builds on earlier research, specifically \cite{bacci:ic3-2017}, and extends its findings by addressing and resolving difficulties encountered in previous studies.

We investigate theoretical the optical properties of quantum-critical geometric phonons within iron-based perovskites. At room temperature, these phonons are inactive but become critical at low temperatures due to the competition between spin and lattice interactions triggered by the presence of magnetic ions. We demonstrate that the resonance of these phonons can occur within the infrared spectrum, coinciding with the absorption of photons by charge carriers, whose increased activity may lead to the suppression of superconductivity through mutual coupling. We compare the phonon's impact on charge carriers to that of ferroelectric transitions in barium titanate, revealing distinct behaviors. Moreover, we discuss the feasibility of modulating geometric phonons via light through the employment of layered calcium-iron arsenide, characterized by two-dimensional electron pockets, and potentially controlling them by applying high pressure to transition metal ions, thereby shifting the resonance to the visible region, potentially resulting in the reemergence of superconductivity accompanied by novel phenomena.

Detecting anomalies in complex multi-dimensional data is a persistent challenge across numerous domains. Current techniques focused on one-dimensional data, such as deep learning-based methods, face significant limitations when dealing with multi-dimensional data, including costly memory and computational requirements. This paper presents an efficient, scalable, and simplified approach to identifying anomalies in multi-dimensional data by converting complex data into distinct closeness graphs and then applying a simple centrality metric to pinpoint abnormal entities. Our method offers unparalleled speed and efficiency when compared to existing alternatives. In our experimental investigation, we analyzed the performance of our methodology on data from the MUGD dataset and the NASA's Zimbra email dataset under both real and synthetic anomalies. Our findings demonstrate the effectiveness of our methodology in detecting anomalies and highlight its superiority in terms of computational speed and precision over traditional methods.

The interaction between an moving atom and its surrounding electromagnetic field plays a crucial role in various quantum processes, as does the response of this field to the moving atom, which influences the observed outcomes. To demonstrate this, a quantum mechanical model is developed for an atom composed of a single proton and a electron cloud spanning several Bohr orbits, which interacts with a nearby mirror. This model shows that the moving atom can stimulate photon emission even when standing waves are not present, and that this emission can be impacted by the atom's charge distribution. Additionally, when a electron jumps from a higher to a lower energy state, a beam of electrons can emerge from the atom-mirror system, where the slim mirror acts as a 180-degree polarized electron mirror.

The assessment of graph understanding, which measures a graph's ability to capture and retain complex information like node characteristics and pairwise relationships, has been long-theorized but remains poorly understood in terms of its exact composition. By defining the injective version of the square of the cut-off graph Laplacian, which better captures local community structures than its non-injective counterpart, we demonstrate how to effectively evaluate a graph's ability to hold localized information within equitable subgroups. Our analysis reveals that equitable partitions can be used not only to measure how well a graph retains its local structure but also to refine community detection by first identifying the smallest subgroups where features are preserved, thus enabling community equity detection. Furthermore, our characterization of injective graphs under specific conditions provides insights into the practical limitations of storing a graph's local information. Our numerical experiments support and extend our theoretical findings. Our developed code will be publicly available for others to build upon.

This research focuses on retreating to earlier therapeutic approaches by analyzing kinetic equations for reversible enzyme reactions from a perspective informed by decision theory. It draws parallels between the behavior of enzymes and decision-making processes, and applies the principle of minimum uncertainty as a criterion for selecting a specific iterative estimation method. By incorporating this criterion, we derive an appropriate estimator choice that analyzes the mean square error of potential estimators and selects one that minimizes uncertainty. Our study delivers formulas grounded in theoretical frameworks, alongside corresponding numerical results, for the case where the rate constants for forward and reverse reactions are known. It also explores scenarios where the ratio of these constants, rather than their individual values, is the relevant parameter. In addition to reevaluating existing estimators, we introduce novel approaches inspired by the method of molecular dynamics simulation. They involve combining reaction-dynamics schemes with equivalent static equations to understand their behavior, and dividing the time evolution into discrete segments based on stochastic dynamics to comprehend steady-state conditions. We investigate the behavior of these estimators using mean field and central limit theory.

A extreme model involving two types of supersymmetry has been examined for 13 TeV proton-proton collisions generated using simulated data and the MadGraph5\_aMC@NLO model. The research investigated diverse final states resulting from the production of supersymmetric particles decaying into distinct particles. The simulated events were compared with actual collision events collected by the CMS experiment between 2016 and 2018. The contrast between predicted and observed data was used to determine the sensitivity of various final states to different supersymmetric particle scenarios. The findings highlight the strength of three specific scenarios: low-mass splittings between neutralinos and charginos, significant mass differences between gluinos and neutralinos, and large mass disparities between heavy gluinos and neutralinos. The research also identified two weakly constrained scenarios: minimal supersymmetry models with high-mass splittings and long-lived particles, and natural supersymmetry models with small mass differences and stable particles. The former scenario was ruled out based on the presence of particles that do not have transverse momentum in certain final states, while the latter was not directly excluded, although some final states appeared less sensitive to the associated supersymmetric properties. The actual limits on the masses of supersymmetric particles were determined and the consistency of the actual data with the predicted supersymmetric model was statistically validated. The validation revealed modest constraints on the masses of particles in the model with small mass differences and stable particles. In the context of financial markets, modeling the expectations of active market participants can provide valuable insights for investing and risk assessment. This can be achieved through the application of probabilistic expectations theories, such as the Quantum Expectation Equilibrium League, which promotes market stability by ensuring expectation mismatches are compensated by relevant financial assets. Consequently, understanding the nature of market participant expectations is of primary interest to asset managers and financial policymakers.

We present a multi-agent market platform enabling the study of market participant expectations, with their expectations fluctuating randomly and means oscillating around a mean-reverting equilibrium. The platform's analysis reveals that the stochastic variation in expectations leads to periodic deviations in asset prices, while increased uncertainty among participants disrupts the efficiency of price durations, ultimately exacerbating financial complexities. The findings suggest that asset managers and policymakers should strive to maintain a stable market environment, mitigating the influence of uncertainty to ensure optimal financial interactions.

This research paper explores the trajectory of a harmonically oscillating particle that gains additional momentum through conservation, accompanied by a localized spike in potential, mimicking the behavior of a propelled harmonic oscillator. The investigation relied on a partial wave function analysis that splits the phase space into discrete regions. Utilizing a Monte Carlo-based approach, the wave function's asymptotic behavior could be accurately determined. The method successfully yielded reliable results including eigenvalues, bracketed error margins, and pure states comprising the eigenfunctions. The paper includes a detailed explanation of the computational algorithm and supports the findings with graphical visualizations.

Recent ground-breaking research in natural language processing has successfully applied sentiment analysis to enhance various recommendation systems, particularly by merging text data with user interests and item attributes. In this research, we focus on enhancing opinion mining in recommender systems by developing a model that accurately analyzes the significance of opinions regarding user satisfaction, leading to improved recommended items. By incorporating the views of others, we introduce a model that successfully predicts opinions expressed by users, demonstrating the outstanding performance of this model in various real-world scenarios. Unlike existing methods that merely analyze sentiment, our novel approach employs an interactive model that successfully captures the relational meaning of text data, resulting in the notable improvement of opinion accuracy. Additionally, our model has lower computational requirements than previous approaches.

Data augmentation methods that incorporate code-switched text significantly boost the accuracy of machine learning models by enabling them to process mixed language inputs. To take advantage of these models, generated synthetic data should mimic natural patterns of code-switching found in authentic text. Therefore, this research aims to investigate the utilization of lexical substitution for generating Arabic-English code-switched text to enhance data availability. We examined all possible lexical substitution methods in CSASyn, evaluating their effectiveness based on contrasting datasets. Notably, our study revealed that utilizing lexical substitution on discourse markers led to the highest gains in test data similarity, estimated to be around 35% to 40%. We also observed substantial improvements in synthetic data quality from replacing Lexical Substitution Method (LSM) results with more accurate instances of code-switching using co-switch probability models. We discussed the challenges and advantages of utilizing LSms in data augmentation and integrated our findings with the CSASyn framework to create a complete data augmentation process.

We show that any infinite collection of surface homeomorphisms whose uniform topological conjugacy classes do not collapse is never compact in the Roelcke topology, extending a result previously achieved with surface automorphisms. Furthermore, the set of isotopy classes of surface homeomorphisms falls apart under the weak topology, answering a 2002 query by Glasscock. Moreover, the established result leads to proof of two earlier conjectures: the union of almost automorphisms' groups across all dimensions is disconnected and the group of surface homeomorphisms' isotopy classes does not include any compact components.

Systems defined by the combination of generalized inverse M\"obius transformations and fractional Laplacian are investigated. Specifically, we identify integrable membrane equations within these systems, showing how their soliton solutions behave under a transformation that results in a set of semi-Lump equations.

The measurement of tetrahedral mesh quality can be calculated in several ways, 
each time less accurate than the previous, when switching from a coarse 
baseline with many tetrahedra to subsequent refinements. We measure the 
amount of inaccuracy introduced at each level of refinement when using 
the edge split method to measure tetrahedral mesh quality. Since the baseline 
is inherently coarse with 107 tets/hex, further reductions result in less 
precise measurements. Despite the limitations, high-quality meshes with 
better precision are achievable through customized algorithms that cut tets 
off tetrahedral layers, especially when utilizing a proprietary mesh 
editor called Mesher. We also provide and distribute this editor along with 
the code used for the experiments reported in this paper on GitHub under the 
name TetsWithMesher.

The relation discovery task involves identifying relationships between entities in knowledge graphs, despite never having seen the involved entities before. To tackle this challenge, the field of relation extraction has explored various methods, including utilizing distant supervision, which directly links entities from a knowledge graph without the need for initial training. However, the approaches currently employed tend to lack the diversity of relationships that might be identified between two entities, mainly due to the way examples are grouped together during training. To address this issue, our research introduces a novel technique that involves training two networks in unison - one for predicting whether two entities are connected in a graph and another for discovering new relationships between entities given the predicted connection. Notably, our method outperforms the state-of-the-art results on three benchmark knowledge graphs.

A significant challenge in reinforcement learning is dealing with high-dimensional state and action spaces. While previous work has focused on properties of metric spaces related to continuity, this research investigates a different aspect of metric space properties relevant to reinforcement learning. We examine if algorithms can rely on less stringent conditions than continuity, specifically weak metrics, to achieve near-optimal results. We demonstrate that this is possible in weakly continuous Markov decision processes under the condition of upper bounded rewards. Our approach introduces new notions: weak metric action weak continuity and weak metric state action continuity. We develop reward upper bound techniques that are useful even in cases with unknown rewards. We show that these results hold for both tabular and function approximations using weakly continuous metrics. Ultimately, we extend value and policy iteration to work with these new metric properties and provide a framework for applying these methods generally.

Arrangements of animacy can significantly affect the recognition of objects in visual tasks, but the specific mechanisms by which these arrangements are evaluated are still unclear. In particular, it's been discovered that the primary visual cortex of humans processes animacy arrangements consistently, regardless of complexity, yet responses vary based on the direction of arrangement patterns. We investigated this further, identifying that animacy arrangements involving straightforward patterns (such as horizontal or vertical) trigger more active responses in the ventral visual cortex compared to arrangements with diagonal or alternating patterns. Notably, complex arrangements with horizontal or vertical patterns are recognized more easily by the ventral visual cortex, especially in processing complex images. These findings reveal that the ventral visual cortex uses multiple complex mechanisms to analyze the arrangements, one of which involves detecting orientation repeats. This orientation repeat mechanism could be an essential component of how animals recognize objects.

Numerical simulations involving partial differential equations (PDEs) play a vital role across various fields by modeling how physical systems change over time. These systems can involve interconnected components, such as heat transfer or fluid dynamics, requiring the simulation of multiple interconnected PDEs. To enhance accuracy, researchers typically refine these simulations by increasing the granularity of the spatial and temporal data used. However, this process generates a vast number of equations that must be solved efficiently to be practical. Unfortunately, the widespread approach to solving these simulations - using an iterative non-Newtonian solver in conjunction with an adaptive finite element method - often results in inaccurate results due to the presence of numerically unstable features. To address these stability issues, the researchers propose an innovative framework for maintaining the desired structure in these simulations. By reformulating the simulation equations to emphasize key characteristics and leveraging specialized optimization algorithms, the method achieves improved stability. The effectiveness of this structure-preserving approach is demonstrated using 1D and 2D numerical case studies, which show its potential to accurately represent interconnected PDE systems while upholding important physical constraints.

We analyzed a specific type of episode from the gamma-ray burst of MAXI J1535-571 observed by Insight-HXMT, focusing on the evolution of its corona and surrounding area. The 1-second resolution data revealed that the corona underwent significant changes, expanding and then shrinking several times in a relatively short period. The outer edge of the corona appeared to stabilize at a specific radius, whereas its inner boundary displayed more complexity. Notably, the brightest area was not at the center of the corena but rather in an area between the outer edge and the inner boundary of the corona, specifically between 20-40 and 10-20 gravitational radii, depending on the specific episode.

In collaborative training, the response of the teaching agent towards students significantly impacts their learning speed and accuracy, yet its natural behavior often hampers students' ability to master complex tasks quickly. To address this concern, we introduced a novel algorithm that exploits social incentives to modify the teaching agent's behavior, promoting students to master complex tasks efficiently by encouraging teachers to focus on easy tasks early on and gradually move to more complex ones as students demonstrate improved performance. Through simulations in the IBM knowledge acquisition cube, our findings show that this social Inherent Motivation of Transfer Enablement (IME) not only accelerates students' convergence to optimal performance but also enhances their robustness against potential disruptions.

We've developed an innovative, efficient method for training unsupervised vision models to identify diverse substances in real-time, regardless of location or conditions. Our approach leverages a unique combination of a data-driven visualisation technique called PLVs and a contrastive learning strategy to handle complex, variable data. To address data complexity, we use a two-stage training process: first, we train the model using a moving average of pre-trained features extracted from a base model, and then refine it using optimized pairs of similar and dissimilar data. To ensure physical consistency, we train and test the model using both physical principles and synthetic data. Our method successfully enhances the performance of pre-trained models across various applications. Furthermore, we apply our method to develop a lightweight, efficient multi-chemist model that accurately identifies multiple elements. Our results are consistently at or near peak performance, according to multiple evaluation metrics, indicating a significant improvement over individual models.

Two-algebras with Lie integration to 2-groups, first defined by Baez and Crans (2005), have garnered significant interest in recent years, due to their relevance to higher categories, particularly crossed modules and nonabelian cohomology, as well as their rich cultural and physical analogies. A significant amount of research is still needed to fully explore the two-algebra structure. This work aims to achieve a comprehensive understanding of 2-group Lie integration and its underlying two-algebras via the Baez-Crans theorem and the adjoint functor approach of Christie. The paper reviews the method employed by the first author to categorify abelian line integrals and examines the two-algebras resulting from the integration of Lie 2-groups via diffusions on algebras, as described by the second author. Our findings also show that under specific conditions, the algebraic structure of Lie 2-groups is consistent with those of generalized E-homotopy groups, as proposed by Baez-Rosenthal. This work will ultimately serve as a valuable resource for those seeking to learn about 2-group Lie integration and its broader field of two-algebras.

We introduce a novel method for detector-free regional feature matching using a transformer-based approach, termed LoFTR. This method employs a hierarchical reconstruction strategy to align regional features with pixel-wise precision, leveraging the coordination capabilities of transformers to achieve high accuracy even with coarser initial alignment. Leveraging the capabilities of patchwise convolutional networks to generate rich feature representations, LoFTR surpasses current state-of-the-art methods in both the wild and with synthetic data, showcasing exceptional performance on established benchmarks such as Nornalized Cut-pair (NC-pair), Deep Features (DF), and SuperGlue. Furthermore, LoFTR exhibits superior real-time performance, capable of processing 640x480 pixel images at approximately 6 frames per second on standard hardware.

This study examines the impact of filter singularity, a prevalent issue in vector magnetic field data, particularly in its appearance and effects on bias derivation. It appears most notably in beta-value spaces used for singularity avoidance techniques but can also occur with less severity in other configurations. The research develops a bias correction model incorporating filter singularity, incorporates it into the delta-Alpha effect model, and suggests its application to beta-value configurations to mitigate this phenomenon, thereby facilitating more accurate magnetic field predictions and decision-making in various applications.

This research paper presents an innovative, non-centralized approach to manage smart grids using smart inverter controls and real-time billing of load through an efficient, game-theoretic method. A novel aggregative game method is employed to determine the optimal level of flexibility in demand response and to calculate the optimal price of flexibility, which can be used to schedule flexible loads based on current energy demand. A learning dynamics technique is utilized to demonstrate the convergence of solutions to the Nash equilibrium of the game, and thorough simulations are conducted to verify the effectiveness and benefits of this approach for maintaining power balance and reducing peak electricity demand.

A more accurate description of gravity is offered by Rastall theory which modifies the Einstein general relativity by introducing an additional divergence-free covariant derivative of the Tμν tensor. Using this theory in black hole physics, we solve the spherically symmetric black hole equation and derive the Hawking temperature for nonrotating and charged black strings. Our analysis includes the impact of both charge and the Rastall parameter on the gravitational field, which in turn affects the black string's horizon location and radius. Furthermore, we express the Rastall parameter in terms of the charge and horizon parameters. Additionally, we calculated the and its influence on near-horizon energy behavior. Moreover, we assumed that the thermal flux is solely a result of the black string horizon, which in turn allows us to infer the impact of the Rastall term on the black string's Hawking temperature. Our analysis also reveals the relationship between the Rastall and electric charges in relation to the black string's Hawking temperature.

We establish a single condition that enables the identification of metrics with comparable convergence speeds in von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem. This condition is specifically related to the unitary system's spectral decomposition. Moreover, our result can be applied to establish the equivalence of metrics in conjunction with weak convergence. Alongside this, we provide concrete instances illustrating the significance of the ergodicity of the group in determining convergence speeds.

The research on extremely metal-poor stars is crucial to understanding the early universe and initial star formation processes. To find more of these stars, we developed a spectral analysis technique using Gaia's BP/RP spectra, which enables the identification of metal-poor stars with surface temperatures between 4000K and 6500K. This technique accurately measures iron abundance with a precision of 0.3 dex and is capable of detecting stars with iron abundance as low as -2.5 when the surface temperature is around 4000K. Through testing, we found that our technique is 90% effective at finding metal-poor stars with iron abundance lower than -1.0 when the surface temperature is above 6500K, but this value needs to be adjusted according to the BP/RP's wavelength calibration and surface temperature. To further improve our technique, we recommend using additional information from the PRISM spectra to find more metal-poor stars, especially those with iron abundance lower than -2 and temperatures ranging from 4000K to 6500K.

This research evaluates and forecasts the severity of the blaze season globally.
The study analyzes data on wildfires from various sources, including the NASA 
Earth Observations dataset, to measure season intensity as average monthly fire
activity across regions and decades. By identifying common patterns in fire
activity across nations, a time-series prediction model utilizing a dynamic
process is established to forecast fire activity. By extrapolating fire activity
trends into the future, this model facilitates preparedness and decision-making 
for wildfire mitigation efforts in the coming season. The model's accuracy is 
verified through historical data analysis, and its potential is further explored 
for predicting upcoming blaze seasons.

The study of linguistic complexity has gained momentum with the development and application of numerous metrics, although the connections between these measures and the underlying aspects of language remain unclear. In an effort to address this, researchers proposed seven corpus-based indices of linguistic complexity, focusing on aspects such as phonology, grammar, syntax, and morphology. These indices were compared across 40 languages using multiple variables, including phonology, grammar, syntax, and morphology. In addition, four existing measures of morphological complexity were compared and correlated with relevant linguistic characteristics, including mean word length, the number of morphs per word, and a morph length distribution parameter. Findings indicate significant correlations between the proposed indices and the variables representing phonology, grammar, syntax, and morphology, particularly in regards to morph length, number of morphs per word, and average word length. It was also discovered that four of the proposed indices are significantly related to mean word length and the number of morphs per word, mirroring the results of a previous investigation. Consequently, it is suggested that these indices are authentic representations of these aspects of linguistic complexity.

We're studying galaxy interactions in the context of self-interacting dark matter, focusing on a method where a smaller galaxy creates gravitational lensing in a more massive galaxy. This method is useful because it doesn't depend on the dark matter distribution, instead relying solely on baryons. Our investigation centers around strong lensing in the Coma galaxy cluster, where we examine lensed sources and their subhalo's impact on the larger structure. Ultimately, our analysis could provide a way to estimate the velocity dispersion of subhalos, which might be difficult to accomplish through direct observation.

Dynamic models commonly used to forecast and analyze real-world phenomena are often challenging to manage once they've expanded beyond a manageable size. This issue is also present in other types of models (e.g. structural equations). Traditionally, model reduction has been difficult because there wasn't a clear understanding of what constitutes a "good" reduction. However, by focusing on key model components (with large influences), researchers can effectively limit complex models and preserve their accuracy. This technique is known as "simplification to focus." Simplification to focus is particularly useful for dynamic models, and can be utilized as a pre-processing step for data visualization, fault detection, and other tasks that become difficult with large models.

This paper proposes the autonomous analysis (AA) of M-ar-K-Fast, a variant of the
arithmetic hidden Markov model (AHMM). The model's combined use of arithmetic
transitions and state emissions facilitates the processing of both continuous and
discrete data. We have developed the M-ar-K-Fast AAs to independently estimate each
model component. Evaluating the M-ar-K-Fast AAs on a diverse set of first-order
models demonstrated their superiority over conventional approaches, achieving an
average error reduction of 50%. The results also revealed the stability of the AAs 
and their compatibility with hidden state and model structure estimation techniques.

Social media platforms are flooded with an immense volume of daily posts from users equipped with smartphones, generating an array of fascinating data encompassing geographical information, visual images, and acoustic signatures. Every second, a considerable number of social media users identify an intriguing event and tag it with geographical information, creating a temporal archive of real-time social media data. In this paper, we present an innovative framework that extracts acoustic signatures from geotagged social media posts, allowing users to navigate and track events through interactive spatial-temporal interfaces in real-time. By leveraging the combination of CNN and LSTM models, our framework accurately identifies real-time events, surpassing existing methods in performance. To cater to the evolving demands of event tracking, we have incorporated three novel interfaces: a map-based interface that enables users to visualize events within specified regions, a timeline-based interface that displays events chronologically, and a 3D scatterplot that presents events in relation to geographical locations and time. The experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in real-time event tracking.

This article examines elliptic equations within the context of a Riemannian surface. It begins with an elliptic equation on a compact Riemannian surface, whose symmetric 2-tensor depends on a parameter, and provides standard results regarding the existence and uniqueness of solutions under generic parameters. The paper proceeds to discuss topological constraints, asymptotic behavior, and signs, as well as the relationship between solutions and metrics, and concludes by presenting a concrete example illustrating non-trivial metrics arising from the solutions.

Advanced cobalt-based materials called YCoB $n$ have garnered significant attention due to their unique properties, where $n$ represents the number of cobalt layers. Researchers have previously focused on the YCoB$_2$ system with the rock-salt structure, but its antiferromagnetic properties limit its practical applications. By employing the Genetica algorithm, combined with the local structure search tool, to screen antiferro- and ferromagnetic systems with the rock-salt structure, a range of cobalt abundant materials were discovered. These materials, referred to as YCoB $n$, have multiple cobalt layers (n ranging from 3 to 15), along with other related compounds such as Zr$_{1-x}$Y$_{1+x}$Co$_4$ ($0\leq x\leq 0.33$ and $x=0.33$) that were proposed based on the binary system with cobalt in excess. Calculations revealed the structural and magnetic properties, including the cohesive energy, lattice parameter, and magnetic ordering, for each compound. By analyzing the results, it is suggested that these newly discovered compounds with the perovskite-like structure may exhibit better ferromagnetic properties than previously thought, which could extend to the YCoB$_2$ system as well. Furthermore, these compounds show potential as promising candidates for further research due to their promising results.

In the display advertising industry, market makers face challenges posed by an unconventional auction mechanism, the Generalized Second Price auction, where the market maker must predict the bidding preference of buyers to calculate an optimal price. Since the auction's winning condition depends on the distribution of the market maker's estimation, rather than the true value, it introduces an inherent bias. We address this issue by presenting an adaptive bidding strategy that adjusts its prediction method in real-time to minimize loss and guarantee a range for the estimated utility. Our approach, tested on real advertising data, demonstrates an impressive performance by surpassing the current best practices in both simulated and real-world scenarios.

We investigate the quantum information properties of a specific two-dimensional nonlinear light beam that emerges from a type of optical device known as an acoustic soliton generator.  Firstly, the paper generates a new mathematical formula that effectively models this phenomenon.  Next, the paper creates a measure to assess the quantum properties of certain optical patterns, such as the unique light patterns generated by the acoustic soliton generator, which is based on the Wigner distribution.  The behavior of this optical pattern when paired with an unrelated optical pattern with certain predetermined characteristics is also analyzed using two established quantum theory frameworks.  The study finds that both these optical patterns exhibit a property called 'nonclassicality' and, additionally, that an increase in this 'nonclassicality' property is associated with an undesirable phenomenon called 'Wigner negativity'.  The impact of 'nonclassicality' on the 'Wigner negativity' property is specifically studied using a type of optical pattern that has an irregular structure.

A crucial element in achieving global security is the establishment of secure quantum key exchange protocols. These protocols ensure that communication key exchange between parties can be carried out safely, without compromising secrecy or falling prey to potential security breaches. This research paper addresses a particular concern related to security breaches involving a quantum key exchange protocol that utilizes an unreliable random source. By modeling this random source as a two-state system with one state being high-quality and secure, and the other state being of lower quality but still non-secure, our study aims to establish a method for determining the exact duration for maintaining security in the quantum key exchange protocol. This is accomplished through a novel model that incorporates a two-state random process, which accurately models the likelihood of obtaining a high-quality random bit at each time step. Our findings provide a precise mathematical expression that can be used to calculate the exact time until the risk of breach increases, thereby serving as a valuable tool for evaluating and assessing the security of quantum key exchange protocols utilizing unreliable random sources. Furthermore, our method can be adapted to other related protocols, including key agreement and distributed key exchange.

This research paper confirms that certain criteria can consistently identify a field of timelike Bertrand curves within a semi-Riemannian manifold. We establish a new method for categorizing these fields, depending on whether they are null or nonnull, and derive explicit criteria for both first and higher-order fields. To illustrate the effectiveness of these results, we provide two specific examples, focused on a three-dimensional hypersurface equipped with a particular metric, and a three-dimensional Euclidean space, respectively.

We explore the connection between the sampling distribution of a Feller diffusion and its stationary distribution. Building upon a novel connection established by Getzler and Sjöstrand in 2001, a more comprehensive relationship is derived through the use of Borel transform and an algebraic geometry approach. This relationship is further generalized to include generalized Hermite polynomials and bi-orthogonal systems, leading to new explicit formulas. The principles discovered are then applied to derive explicit formulas for the sampling distribution of Gaussian processes, leveraging the properties of Feller diffusion equations. The approach is illustrated by deriving explicit formulas for the sampling distribution of certain Hermite-analytic cosocalar processes.

In waveguide pair scattering processes within quantum electrodynamics, an innovative method is introduced that accommodates multiple photon arrangements through the utilization of specific diagrams. This technique effectively handles any number of photon configurations involved in scattering events. Its application starts with a basic unit representing photon creation and interaction, and it uses a combination of rules to ensure consistency in photon numbers. When put to practice, this approach yields results that align with the findings from quantum field theory. Its versatility in dealing with any number of photon arrangements makes it versatile enough to be extended to scenarios involving three waveports and to the scattering of not only individual, but also multiple particle pairs.

A hidden sector containing spin-1 particles can serve as the perfect setting for explaining away anomalous present-day signals of dark matter that exceed expectations. By allowing these particles to efficiently interact with their dark matter counterparts, their abundance can be increased, potentially aligning with parity symmetry within the hidden sector. This increased abundance has the added effect of amplifying standard selfannihilation signals by several orders of magnitude. Our focus lies in the more suppressive scenario of dark matter selfannihilation at smaller distances within hidden matter, rather than the more dominant selfannihilation process occurring at large distances. This model also proposes a supplementary interaction allowing dark matter particles to be accompanied by hidden spin-1 particles. The associated dark matter particles are only lightly bound to their respective centers of mass, allowing them to exhibit a weakly bound haloes properties characteristic of fiducial selfannihilation products. They may also facilitate a faster diffusion into the centers of stars, enabled by the exchange of these light particles between dark matter particles and the sun, potentially resolving the issue of $\mathcal{O}(1)$ solar $^7$Be decay problems. Our analysis reveals that a previously neglected channel plays a dominant role in the diffusion process, however this new information also shows that the associated particles have properties distinct from those of charginos, which could make them identifiable at the LHC.

This note employs Bernoulli polynomials and their derivatives to illustrate and prove Faulhaber's Formula for the sum of the $n$th power of consecutive integers, along with a related generalization discovered by Stanislaw Ulam.

Continuous phase modulation, popular in wireless systems due to its simple
non-linear characteristics and high spectral efficiency, is traditionally detected
using a non-coherent method which calculates the phase shift between reception
signals and a known signal pattern. Despite its simplicity, this detection method
is susceptible to a problem known as cycle slip, which occurs when the phase
calculation indicates an unfeasible phase shift. To mitigate this issue, phase
correction methods are employed, which significantly complicate the system and
add considerable processing delays. In this research, it is demonstrated that the
existence of cycle slips does not have a detrimental impact on a specific type of
modulated CPM, which can thus avoid the need for complex and delayed
correction methods. This study confirms that uncorrected CPM detection is a
plausible option for this specific type of CPM, which is known as multi-tone CPM.

In reward learning, reward functions are taught to be applied to real-world situations, making them very useful in tasks like autonomous decision-making and policy implementation. However, defining reward functions can be very challenging and requires significant expertise. Reward learning aims to simplify this process by allowing these functions to be learned from examples and their corresponding ratings. One way to make reward learning more efficient is to combine it with clustering techniques. This approach groups examples into categories and lets an expert prioritize them, making the learning process much faster. However, most existing methods with clustering techniques have two main problems: (1) they don't take into account expert's preferences when grouping examples and (2) they don’t always use the expert’s preferences effectively. (3) Also, the learning algorithms are not always used efficiently. We propose a new fully automated method that uses the expert’s preferences to group examples and rank them. This method uses visual support to simplify this process and reduce the complexity of defining reward functions. It also uses the the the Bregman distance to measure how similar each group is, and to determine which examples should be grouped together based on the the the target reward distribution. This method performs very well in real-world experiments, and it’s much faster than other methods in the field.

Within the noncommutative spacetime framework, based on the Zee model, a new theoretical approach has been developed to describe nucleon composition in terms of quark distributions using operator products. This novel method enables the derivation of parton distribution functions (PDFs) with noncommutative spacetime effects considered, and it aligns with the principle that PDFs are invariant under the commutative spacetime rearrangement. Consequently, the calculated PDFs exhibit noncommutative spacetime effects, leading to notable changes, particularly in the gluon composition of protons at the Zee level, where the impact is more pronounced at high $B$ values, and further experiments are needed to distinguish between the new and traditional PDFs.

Research on two-dimensional quantum systems has reached new heights, driven by the unique characteristics of quantum topology. The search for diverse quantum phenomena remains an ongoing challenge, and recent findings from exact numerical calculations on two-dimensional quantum models reveal substantial topological effects sparked by quantum frustration. The results focus on quantum spin models, specifically the triangular lattice quantum dimer model and the recently introduced triangular lattice quantum anisotropy model, which exhibit significant topological behavior. The calculations show the presence of a novel topological edge in both models, and the associated phase diagrams accurately predicted the occurrence of topological states through numerical analysis, the Monte-Carlo method, and the quantum loop operator technique. The findings from these studies could lead to new applications in quantum materials research and related fields.

We examine the spectral properties of large, randomly constructed Hermitian matrices, specifically those with off-diagonal elements that follow a Gaussian distribution, as the size of the matrices approaches infinity. By considering matrices of finite rank that incorporate a real diagonal component, we derive a closed-form expression for the expectation of the largest eigenvalue in terms of a scalar integral involving the underlying underlying two-point correlation function. Additionally, we investigate the asymptotic behavior of Green's function and show that its magnitude decreases as 1/\sqrt{N}, where N represents the dimension of the matrices, courtesy of a modified sigma-model. Moreover, we estimate the statistical error associated with the estimation of the spectral measure, revealing an order of 1/\sqrt{N} times a logarithmic term. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings in relation to recent numerical experiments.

Recent advancements in pre-trained conversational language models have achieved state-of-the-art results in various conversation understanding tasks. Nevertheless, conventional approaches lacking a clear semantic foundation tend to yield incomplete and inaccurate comprehension results. This research proposes an innovative method for pre-training conversational models through the extraction of vital information - context - which enables accurate conversation comprehension. Our proposed model, named Meaningful Conversation Pre-training (MCP), incorporates a multi-faceted architecture to capture context, consisting of a multi-layered syntax-based dependency extraction model and a multi-task learning framework for capturing context through syntax-guided meaning representation. Our comprehensive evaluations demonstrate MCP's superiority over competing models and its exceptional performance on multiple conversation understanding tasks. Additionally, we conduct an in-depth analysis to reveal insights into its internal workings. Our source code has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/rgelim/Transformer-Multitask-MRC.

Machine learning algorithms achieve transparency through explainable AI, but their usability varies based on individual comprehension levels. To address this, a new approach is proposed, focusing on how people learn to understand the outcomes of these algorithms. This involves defining three key principles: transparency, learnability, and usability. The first principle requires that there be a method for providing overall insight into an algorithm's operation. The second principle specifies that understanding an algorithm's process becomes gradually more achievable as training progresses. The third principle concerns the time it takes for humans to acquire the necessary knowledge to effectively apply an algorithm. This leads to the development of a measure to assess how easily people can learn from and understand algorithms, quantified by the "cognitive complexity score." Studies have shown that when humans are presented with algorithms that are designed to be easily learned (through visualization, step-by-step explanations, and correct ordering), their cognitive complexity score is very low. In contrast, humans who try to make sense of opaque models (such as neural networks) have a high cognitive complexity score. This difficulty for humans to understand models of their own accuracy is connected to a decline in their trust in AI. As a result, it is recommended that AI systems be designed not only to be increasingly understandable but also progressively more learnable and usable by humans, adapting to each individual's cognitive development.

Anomaly detection without the need for labels is an appealing concept in
machine learning, and we've found a simple, efficient, and scalable method to
realize it by utilizing the Isolation Forest (iForest) algorithm. iForest is
based on the principle that isolated objects are easily isolated, and it uses
a binary tree to locate anomalies. However, in certain situations, such as
on low-capacity devices or in environments with limited computational resources,
the method can be too resource-intensive due to overhead calculations. We've also
discovered that the quality of the training dataset may not greatly affect the
accuracy of iForest in label-free scenarios. Based on these findings, we've
created TiWS-iForest, an implementation of iForest optimized for label-free and
resource-constrained environments. The results of our experiments show that
tiws-iForest surpasses state-of-the-art algorithms in both performance and
efficiency on a widely used anomaly detection benchmark.

A novel approach to parameter estimation in extreme value theory involves a more sophisticated model of the processes that generate extreme events. While the classic extreme value theory assumptions often hold, our approach tackles potential violations by modeling event occurrences as Poisson-distributed across distinct areas, allowing for modeling based on both spatial and temporal patterns. We develop a Bayesian estimation method for the model's parameters, which ultimately yields more accurate results. Simulation studies demonstrate that this approach surpasses the traditional method, particularly in scenarios with complex patterns, and we showcase its effectiveness through a real-world analysis of low-probability floods in Spain.

Our previous research established the theoretical underpings for differential cross section formulas, which led to the discovery that the scattering matrix has both quasi-periodic and quasi-constant components.
The quasi-periodic components of the scattering matrix can be characterized by trajectories in momentum space that exhibit periodic deviations. 
The areas associated with constant cross sections correspond to trajectories with no deviation at fixed impact parameters.
Several models, including those derived from strong absorption and shallow potentials, demonstrate the existence of constant cross section areas.
Furthermore, our results indicate that quasi-periodic cross section variations occur in adjacent cells of a discrete momentum grid and reach their maximum amplitude at half sampling intervals.
The areas of fixed cross sections, denoted as $\Omega_f$, can be identified through the calculation of the scattering matrix along the x-axis in momentum space and its replicas in adjacent cells.
The set of fixed cross section areas, denoted as $\mathfrak{F}$, includes the union of $\Omega_f$ from various cell sub-cells and our model-based testing shows that the total $\Omega_f$ area is significantly larger than the square of the impact parameter.
Therefore, the previously proposed fixed cross section approximation may yield greater accuracy than previously estimated.
Moreover, our analysis suggests that the quasi-constant cross section areas could be optimized by refining the grid sampling interval.
The proposed method can be applied to any effectively integrable system, including those derived from Schrödinger and Hartree-Fock equations, which indicates its broad range of

This research focuses on advancing knowledge representation and extraction, and we've 
developed a dataset, COMET-ATOMIC, comprising 220K atomic actions described using 
fine-grained syntactic structures and encoded in both vector spaces and symbolic 
formats. To demonstrate the potential of combining symbolic and neural computing, 
we've leveraged ATOMIC's fine-grained labels to establish connections between 
words, and developed a neural network that can accurately generate these labels 
from the resulting graph. We've also employed combinatorial algorithms to parse 
the graph and establish an even more refined set of labels. Our results show 
significant improvements in both token and subaction accuracy compared to the 
original predictors used in the COMET challenge.

The \textit{Herschel} Great Galactic Circle Survey's extensive catalogues house an immense number of data, spanning approximately 67,000 sources across 320 $\mu$m, 250 $\mu$m, and spectral energy distribution plots. Managed through the CIRADA Infrared Pipeline (CIRAP), these sources were identified from spatially decomposed data and various infrared maps, utilizing a multi-scale approach for wavelet denoising and source information compression. This approach is pivotal in maintaining data integrity throughout the observation process and facilitates efficient data archiving and distribution at the Herschel Science Centre. Furthermore, the CIRAP has enabled 3D spectral index mapping, which is being utilized to analyze the Serpens North cloud; this technique is significant in determining the properties of local interstellar matter.

We examined the globular cluster NGC2808, rich in magnesium, to understand how its internal dynamics affected the accuracy of star ages and metal compositions. Using the Gaia ephotometry (e=0.03) and high-resolution spectral analysis (E=~70000K), we calculated the cluster's metal composition and elemental ratios with precision. Our analysis showed the presence of an intermixed composition spread, confirmed by the presence of multiple population groups, and determined the cluster's metal composition and helium abundance for different populations. We derived ages, 10.5+/-0.8 Myr, for both red giant He-burning and helium-rich populations, indicating the likelihood of multiple population groups in NGC2808, and indicating that first-generation stars in this cluster survived for an extended period of time.

In an individual's life, the key factor for achieving success is often linked to their ability to escape difficult situations, such as financial struggles or a state of low social standing. This concept is modeled in a one-dimensional growth model where a particle moves forward by stochastic increments. Calculations are specific to the standard normal distribution, determining the probability that a particle fails to exit a defined, limited space within a specified time frame. This is represented as the ratio of two probability integrals, each involving the difference between cumulative distribution functions of the patient $\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$ and the aggressive $\mathcal{N}(2\mu, 4\sigma^2)$ distributions. Furthermore, the aggressive distribution is shifted and scaled. This expression is then analyzed in terms of entropy, and its relation to a measure representing the difference between two distributions is investigated.

Quantum Bayes' Theorem has been verified to accurately describe the process of making inferences in quantum physics. However, the application of numerical methods in calculating conditional probabilities raises concerns about whether numerical methods or the underlying Bayes' Theorem framework is responsible for validating quantum principles. To address these concerns, we employed an analytical solution previously developed by one of the authors within the framework of Quantum Bayes' Theorem for a specific class of problems. Our findings indicate that the validity of quantum principles, in particular, the preservation of non-zero probabilities for continuous variable measurements, is a consequence of the underlying Bayes' Theorem framework utilized to derive the conditional probabilities. This confirms that the quantum generalization of Bayes' Theorem has the capacity to validate fundamental aspects of quantum physics.

The thermodynamic properties of QCD are examined through the lens of complex systems theory, revealing a unique phase structure that differs significantly from the commonly assumed deconfined-hadronic phase structure. Instead, it exhibits multiple confinement thresholds giving rise to distinct Major and minor states of the theory. These minor states include a multitude of quasi hadronic, quasi quark and antiquark, quark-antiquark, polyquark, and hybrid hadronic states that exist at higher temperature and chemical potential compared to their confined counterparts. In the context of high-energy interactions, minor systems play a pivotal role and are fundamentally linked to the concept of multicolor confinement. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the equation of state derived from QCD's minor phase is consistent with lattice simulations, whereas the hadronic black hole phenomenon at high temperature and zero baryon chemical potential was recently discovered.

The Steenrod algebra's $A'(q)$ cohomology is studied with unspecified characteristics $q$. It has been discovered that some cohomology elements within the $A'(q)$ cohomology's decomposed components show a distinct dependence on $q$, despite initially appearing to be universally present across all $q$. By examining the $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$-graded cohomology, specific Steenrod algebra cross-structures can be reconstructed, and new computations involving truncated polynomial algebras from May are used to determine critical components within the $A'(q)$ cohomology's decomposed structure. These new findings include the identification of additional cross-structures and Ring Spectra computations related to $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$-graded cohomology also providing insights into the decomposed cohomology's structure, specifically in how its cross-structures span across different $q$. This analysis ultimately serves as a basis to examine the Steenrod algebra's cohomology across broad classes of rings. The paper also includes an accompanying appendix presenting a computational software program designed to determine cohomology decompositions for specific Steenrod algebra constructions across various rings.

The Lyman ultraviolet spectral region holds significant importance in astronomy due to the prominent Lyman-alpha (Ly$\alpha$) absorption features seen in every galaxy's interstellar medium. However, Lyman-alpha screens with centennial transmission are now being applied in various spectroscopic projects to eliminate Ly$\alpha$ contamination and ensure the transmission stability required for precise Lyα observation. In this study, we examine the Lyα screen's impact on photometric accuracy using a Ly$\alpha$ screen in the case of an ultraviolet spectrograph. To achieve this goal, we perform photometric measurements of several standard stars using the Lyα screen, comparing these values with those obtained through a clean glass on the same instrument. Our data show that by using the Lyα screen, the ultraviolet flux is decreased by approximately 2 percent, in contrast to the stable flux (within the 0.5 percent margin of error) obtained with the clean glass. In summary, a Lyα screen decreases the ultraviolet by around 2 percent, in line with our prior knowledge. In addition, we examine potential alternatives to Lyα screens, proposing that by using ultraviolet spectroscopy with medium-resolution spectrometers in the 300-400 nm wavelength range, standard stars can be identified with nearly the same accuracy as with photometric methods. In the final section, we discuss the implications of these findings for ongoing and future missions such as MOAST, HST, and JWST.

This paper addresses the problem of managing an identity graph for Graph Symmetric Networks through a distributed controller. The controller can utilize an arbitrary connected graph as a network device to achieve identity construction, but it must ensure that the resulting graph's properties are uniform across all its nodes. A set of rules for configuring the network device has been established and proof of these rules' effectiveness has been provided. Furthermore, a method of implementing the controller using reversible logic gates in a specific device model has been presented and its operation has been formally demonstrated.

Our work centers on developing an image cataloging system utilizing Distributed Hash Tables (DHTs), particularly suitable for distributed systems lacking central administrative control. By utilizing a DHT, we alleviate the need for centralized infrastructure. The proposed cataloging system utilizes image hashes generated through perceptual hashing as its primary data storage component. Due to varying image hash properties, we've identified challenges including caching inconsistencies, hash variations, and caching truncation. To overcome these issues, we've implemented a two-stage hashing approach, combining time-based caching for enhanced performance, and employed caching techniques to mitigate the effects of varying hash properties and caching limitations. The Supertree method has been incorporated to address caching truncation issues. This system's primary contribution lies in its capability to dynamically maintain and update catalogs, facilitated by the rapid insertion and deletion of image entries.

This study verifies the feasibility of a novel, unsupervised approach to error correction for binary linear codes within Gaussian noise. The developed algorithm, drawing on ideas from combinatorial optics and differential geometry, does not require initial transmission of encoded data, instead using received signals as its starting point to create a map representing likelihoods of noise and channel distance. By analyzing this map, the algorithm estimates the binary state of the data and a binary matrix representing the code, enabling it to perform decoding. However, empirical results presented in this study indicate that this method, although theoretically viable, is impractical due to the extremely high computational demands required, with the rate of code transmission approaching zero as the length of the code grows.

We analyze the movement of a particle under the influence of a specific potential, referred to as the washboard potential, when its velocity remains constant. The conditions necessary for an accelerated, dispersion-free movement are derived exactly, as well as a detailed analysis of the resulting motion, using both a generalized Lagrangian approach and a Hamiltonian formalism. The findings are further validated by introducing a new ordinate variable. The study also explores the general characteristics of the particle's trajectory and discusses its implications in a practical context.

High-precision location and speed evaluation of moving objects is crucial in various unmanned systems, particularly robotics, autonomous vehicles, and unmanned aerial vehicles. The history of localization techniques spans several decades, with the problem being how to best utilize available sensor data, including lidar, radar, and cameras, to facilitate localization. The straightforward approach of directly relating sensor data to position and speed is hindered by the system's non-linearity and noise. In this paper, we present a novel adaptable local projection method that utilizes radar data to accurately estimate position and speed by utilising radar's high-resolution range and angular data. The proposed approach first creates a 3D point cloud from radar data and selects corresponding pixels from a mono-camera, aligning them using a general epipolar constraint to estimate the distance and angle of the reflected radiation. The estimated radiation distance and angle are then used to calculate the object's horizontal speed and position, yielding results comparable to those of top-rated deep learning-based and geometric-based methods, with the added advantages of being lightweight, fast, and requiring minimal computational power.

We're conducting a classical study on the quantum void, specifically exploring the angular behavior of a charged particle within a zero-confined space, both as an electron and as part of a larger dipole under the influence of an arbitrary magnetic field, precisely Landau's. This builds upon previous work that investigated the effects of confined space on a charged particle, both as an electron and as part of a larger dipole. This quantum void behavior manifests as an irregular, distorted 2-dimensional continuum, displayed through three-dimensional plots, showing characteristic alluvial curves, especially in the absence of confinement and when the charge's dimensions are large in comparison to the confinement size.

Research in knowledge graph extraction involves a crucial task known as named entity classification (NEC). A recent study proposed the FGNET framework, which used a novel fusion of graph embeddings in Euclidean space to achieve outstanding results. However, graph-based models in Euclidean space have limitations, particularly when dealing with complex knowledge graphs that require more complex structures. This paper addresses these limitations by adapting the FGNET framework to take advantage of hyperbolic geometry, leading to improved NEC performance. To achieve this, a new framework called FGNET-RH was developed, incorporating a reliable hierarchy to facilitate effective training. Experimental results on diverse knowledge graphs, including the Wikipedia KG and FGNET, showcase the superiority of FGNET-RH across various settings.

This paper investigates the relationships between special polynomials with several properties, including those within the unified tangent module and the Szegö class, focusing on the Hankel determinants and the Fej\'er-Riesz norms. We establish the connections between the secondary Hankel determinants and other properties, identify distinct varieties related to these connections, and compare the properties of special polynomials within the unified class and the Szegö class.

In a cloud-based data hub, virtual machines (VMs) are allocated dynamically 
to meet changing workloads, with their numbers often managed by a global 
scheduler. Conversely, storage nodes rely on a fixed number of predefined 
subfolders to maintain consistency across VM placements. To prevent these 
folders from becoming overly loaded and biased towards certain VMs, a new 
schedule-independent partitioning approach is proposed. This approach, named 
Prepartition, dynamically allocates subfolders to VMs while promoting even 
load distribution without favoring specific VMs. Although developed with 
cloud-based data hubs in mind, the proposed method is generally applicable to 
any resource allocation scenario requiring partition-subfolder combinations.

We're focusing on the most basic type of game, where two players apply a combination of strategies and reactions to each other's moves, with the end goal being to predict how these interactions will reach a state of equilibrium. In the past, it was a challenge to create a machine learning model for this type of game, but we're proposing a new method that utilizes a technique called Fixed Point Networks. This approach relies on a type of neural network called GANs, but with the added benefit of ensuring that the output is stable and accurate by keeping an eye on the fixed point equation. Our experiments show that this type of network is capable of successfully forecasting the equilibrium of this type of game, ultimately allowing us to explore more complex questions about its behavior.

In decision theory, the concept of causal influence is crucial for determining how one random variable affects another, even after controlling for other factors. The focus is on developing a definition of partial identification limits for causal influence with applications in high-dimensional data analysis. The definition uses a minimax optimization problem to define the upper and lower bounds of a target parameter. The upper bound involves the minimum over all relevant variables that do not influence the target, while the lower bound involves the minimum over all relevant variables that are influenced by the target. The definition's effectiveness is demonstrated through consistent estimators that converge to the defined upper and lower bounds. The defined bounds can be expanded to more complex models, including those with unobserved confounding variables. The definition's utility is illustrated through its application to a real-world student outcome study where we examine the educational impact of school characteristics on student outcomes. The defined bounds are estimated using neural networks, a type of nonparametric estimator.

We've developed an efficient early warning system for LTI systems being attacked with covert methods. Our main contributions are two-fold. Firstly, we used the Kalman filter to create an unbiased estimate of system state in the presence of hidden attack. The attack model used here assumes that attackers maintain control of the system without detection for a set period of time. Our system also calculates the variance of this state estimate to detect the attack. Secondly, we present a simple yet effective method to calculate the variance of the system state in the presence of hidden attacks. This involves establishing a relationship between the state estimate and the original system state, allowing us to measure the state estimate uncertainty. This method is simple, straightforward, and applicable to standard digital control systems. It also provides accurate early warning without requiring significant modifications to existing control systems.

A language facilitates communication by providing a common understanding among individuals, with spoken languages consisting of sounds and written languages consisting of symbols. English, a widely spoken language, has inherent ambiguities due to its single-word representation, which complicates written expressions. To overcome this, formal grammar and vocabulary are essential for conveying unambiguous meanings. Despite this, natural language processing continues to be a prominent research field, with the goal of developing algorithms to process languages through computers. Our work explores the application of formal grammar in processing languages, particularly in the context of Indian languages where specific facilitators are lacking. We leverage the power of formal system semantics to derive meaningful representations from written texts, thereby extracting summaries from spoken dialogues. Our method is evaluated against other widely-used techniques that rely on external knowledge sources and emotional analysis, with the results demonstrating the superiority of our approach.

We introduce the concept of S-rings of Noether type and demonstrate their prevalence, also characterizing them in specific contexts. Additionally, we establish the, as expected, close connection between right Noetherian S-rings and quasi-Van den Bergh rings. Furthermore, an example is provided of a right Noetherian S-ring that is not subadditive. Moreover, an S-rings analogue of the Doran-Goldie theorem is derived. Lastly, an example is given of a right Noetherian S-ring that lacks the RG property.

Recent research has revealed a increased transverse acceleration within approximately 25 parsecs of our environment, which cannot be fully explained by the dynamic effects of the Roshe indivisibility phenomenon. A reasonable assumption has been put forth that this acceleration could be a result of gravitational influence from unseen companions. This study aims to identify and constrain the parameters of these hidden companions using their accelerated host stars moving within 15 parsecs of our environment. By utilizing the accelerated radial velocities of five nearby stars, including their distances, PMAs, and 2MASS K magnitudes, we performed Brown dwarf and stellar model cross-matching to determine the likely mass ranges for each companion based on their host star's properties. Subsequently, models of space distribution and number density of dwarf stars within 20 parsecs were consulted to constrain the possible companion masses and distances. Ultimately, the companion parameters were refined through a consistency check against the acceleration of the companion star, $\epsilon$ Tuc h, whose parameters were determined as having a mass of 0.025 M$_\odot$, a companion mass of 0.03-0.14 M$_\odot$, a distance of 11.7 parsecs, and a projected mass at a selected location of 0.030 M$_\odot$. The resultant findings indicate that hidden companions consistent with the observed acceleration within 15 parsecs exist at extremely low rates of 0.7-2.0$\times$10$^{-4}$
