The invariant-set concept within concealed-variable theory offers a compelling solution to the problem of quantum nonlocality, effectively circumventing the issue at a fundamental level. Unfortunately, the existing form of this solution necessitates a redefinition of the conventional notion of causality, making it seem likely that the solution itself is also unsound. The present paper explores an alternative formulation of the invariant-set concept within a concealed-variable framework, one that avoids modifying the standard causal order while maintaining it in the concealed-variable context. This new formulation serves as a starting point to address quantum nonlocality, and it is then utilized to develop an explicit model based on Bell's theorem, demonstrating quantum nonlocality even in the local-realistic concealed-variable context of Mach-Zehnder type. In addition, some relevant connections between hidden variables and superdeterminism are established, and it is also shown how the local-realistic concealed-variable model developed in this paper can be regarded as a form of superdeterministic model, revealing that the distinct concepts of quantum nonlocality, superdeterminism, and the invariant-set idea are actually connected in a rather tight manner.

With the rapid advancement in IoT, machine-type communications are projected to outnumber human communications over the network, however, this surge will only be fully realized if the machines are capable of producing valuable data that can be utilized by other machines, humans, or both. For IoT devices to effectively communicate with each other, as well as with humans, an efficient machine-type communication system that can automatically analyze text and extract key phrases is necessary. Our goal is to explore neural networks for processing machine communication language and evaluating the effectiveness of different neural networks in parsing IoT device text, utilizing a dataset of labeled phrases from various domains. Our results demonstrate the potential of neural networks in processing IoT device language and highlight RNNs, which use word dependencies, as a promising model.

We examine the properties of dimer models on random lattices near their critical points and discover that the underlying physics is analogous to the behavior of massless fermions in a non-gauge invariant gauge field. This connection emerges from a novel technique that integrates the exact solving method of the critical dimer model with the approach of Chern-Simons statistics for highly intertwined gauge fields. Applying this method to the case of triangular lattices, we establish that the dimer model on random triangular lattices possesses a topological phase when the number of dimensions is seven, possesses a gapped phase in three dimensions, and displays randomness in two dimensions. This research reveals that the dimer models can serve as a simple and exact model for the low-energy behavior of gauge fields. Additionally, we use our method to derive the statistical properties of Dirac fermions in a non-gauge invariant gauge field, which confirms that the effect of non-invariant flux on fermions is accounted for by the Chern-Simons term.

This paper introduces a enhanced version of the Group Lasso (GL) for the regression analysis of categorical data. Since the conventional GL is prone to neglecting important factors with closely tied coefficients, it is specifically tailored to handle high-dimensional categorical data. To achieve this, a novel enhanced Group Lasso (EGL) is proposed, which implements a novel Group Lasso penalty (GLP) that estimates the conditional probabilities of each level within a categorical variable and uses these to determine the relative importance of the variable. Furthermore, a dual-form EGL (EGLD) is also explored, which is solved through an iterative process of dual updating and primal perturbation. Our research indicates that both the EGL and EGLD algorithms are capable of producing accurate predictions with reduced generalization error, and that the EGLD has a significantly simplified computational complexity compared to other dual-form algorithms. Our method is demonstrated through the analysis of a synthetic dataset and two real-world datasets from the IMDB40 and Metacritic datasets. These results demonstrate the efficacy of this approach for the regression analysis of categorical data, and our code can be found on the GitHub repository at https://github.com/Ahualio/EGL.

In recent years, the development of real-time hypervisors has become a research focus due to their potential in real-time embedded systems. Up to now, most research has been based on x86 architecture, which is often used in servers and desktops, but not typically in embedded devices. This paper presents a new real-time hypervisor, dubbed T-Visor, which is designed to manage mixed-importance embedded real-time systems that utilize hardware virtualization technology. By taking a general embedded environment as its target, T-Visor aims to minimize its overhead, achieving predictable performance even in low-end host CPUs. In experiments, it was found that T-Visor's delay variation is less than 10% and its maximum delay is within the 250 microsecond mark. What's more, T-Visor has successfully passed the RTOS Fitting test with a 0-second error, which indicates T-Visor's real-time capabilities. Compared to existing real-time hypervisors like Xen, QEMU, and rKVM, T-Visor significantly reduces the delay virtualization brings, whether it be the creation or termination of virtual machines or execution within them.

Creating 360-degree panoramic images involves combining multiple partial scenes, a process that is often challenging in real-world applications. Many existing techniques focus on maximizing the depth of the resulting image, but this is not necessarily the best approach, as it can easily lead to distorted partial scenes. In fact, the depth is just one aspect of several possible objectives, including maintaining texture alignment, which is essential for creating a seamless image. Our main contribution is the development of a novel, lightweight algorithm that minimizes texture alignment errors while maintaining image depth, and we also present an enhanced version that incorporates additional motion effects for more natural appearances. Our analysis confirms that our simple yet effective method produces better results than other available techniques, and our code has been made available for others to build upon.

Chimeric synchronizer-free networks, with their irregular complex rhythms, may exist in systems of interconnected oscillators, such as interconnected brain circuits. In chimeras consisting of two populations, one population always remains in synchrony with the other, whereas the other remains asynchronous. However, our research shows that when the bifurcation parameter varies at a certain rate in such a system, chimeras are formed only at specific, even intervals throughout the parameter space, and these rhythms, although complex and varied, follow a predictable pattern of creation and destruction. Furthermore, these findings apply to networks of coupled oscillators of any type, and their validity is also supported by experimental results obtained from pendulum-like systems.

Developing skilled controllers for advanced robotic systems like humanoid robots is an extremely challenging task.  Due to their complex dynamics and broad motion patterns, it's almost impossible for human experts to create a comprehensive and detailed explanation of the desired behavior.  In this research, we introduce a more efficient and effective strategy to design controllers that can withstand disruptions and errors.  By using a simulation-based method, we simulate different possible responses to various robotic movements and train a controller to maintain its target goal by selecting the most likely and safe option among the available options.  We tested this approach on a humanoid robot that navigates through different environments and successfully demonstrated its capability to recover from unexpected disruptions such as sudden changes in momentum and loss of balance.

Multi-layer graphs, which extend standard graph theory to include multiple labeled edge sets, are examined in this study. Each label within a multi-layer graph signifies a specific type of connection, allowing for the creation of a sub-graph composed of only that particular label, known as a slice of the graph. A slice of a multi-layer graph, specifically an elevated slice, is derived by applying a transformation, ensuring it retains the same vertices as the original multi-layer graph. A new algebraic structure, known as the elevated slice algebra, is introduced in this study to analyze elevated slices of graphs. This study will explore the combinatorial properties of this graph structure, which will have practical applications in data analysis of multi-layer graphs, particularly in the study of quantum data.

We explore the relationship between entropy and mutual information in stochastic tensor networks by developing a mirrored structure. This approach leads to an equilibrium condition that mirrors thermodynamic principles, is consistent across multiple entropy definitions, and is applicable to both semi-finite and infinite stochastic tensor networks. In tensor network theory, this framework enables the determination of mutual information and complete entropy in large-scale systems, a feat that was previously achievable only through demanding numerical procedures. We illustrate this point with two exemplary physical scenarios, the first involving the entanglement entropy of the two-dimensional Ising model and the second the entropy of two-dimensional Majorana fermions.

Although initial conditions hold obvious importance in understanding the behavior of deterministic systems, their role in stochastic systems is often ambiguous. By adopting a functional derivative approach to analyze generalized Onsager relations, this research demonstrates the significance of initial conditions in stochastic thermodynamics, particularly in the stochastic dynamics of a widespread class of Markovian systems. These systems include reaction dynamics with multiple species and spatially homogeneous processes. For these general systems, heritable patterns in the equilibrium distribution have a fundamental connection to the initial conditions, as represented by the generalized Onsager coefficients. Importantly, this research shows that patterns which are both heritable and temporally enduring can be reduced to those at equilibrium, as illustrated by applications to Reaction Rate Order and stochastic chemical kinetics in a spatial and temporal context.

The generalized Hénon map, defined by $x_{x_{n+1}}=\beta x_n+\delta x_{n-1}+ax_{n-1}^3$, exhibits complex behavior, especially when parameters $\delta$ and $f$ are varied, leading to the classification of Hénon map diagrams into different regions. These diagrams can either show chaotic behavior with periodic patterns or well-behaved, convergent behavior. However, as the parameters are fine-tuned, a region of indetermination emerges, making the classification of Hénon map diagrams challenging. To address this uncertainty, a new method is proposed. This new approach involves visualizing the attractors of the generalized Hénon map for different values of $\delta$ and $f$. These attractors can be found through the iteration of the generalized Hénon map. Since the generalization doesn't always yield a compact set for the iteration, some attractors may not be available for all parameter values. Results show that the proposed method can help classify the generalized Hénon map diagrams, providing a new perspective on this matter.

Despite its name, gravitational curvature doesn't directly relate to the standard notion of curvature in geometry. Instead, it's a measure of the irregular motion occurring within a celestial system. Just like how the ordinary differential equations for isolated bodies in the standard Newtonian framework eventually converge into solutions resembling Kepler's laws, the irregular motions in these systems can be described by solutions akin to Laplace's continuity equation. This, in turn, leads to a gravitational curvature expression that's reminiscent of the Poisson equation but without its divergent form. This study examines the free version of the continuity equation within a spherical context, where it yields an interesting geometric interpretation involving irrotational vector flows. The solutions obtained can be divided into ordinary hydrodynamic solutions with limited velocity and solitons of the Laplace equation. Solitons come in several forms, such as toroidal bodies and biconics, with biconics having two distinct versions, split, conical, and elliptical. Split and conical shapes represent specific instances of soliton families, with split forms representing reversed torus states and conicals being intermediate forms between them. This study delves into the properties of these shapes and model various celestial bodies. Our exploration also reveals several possibilities for further advancement in understanding gravitational behavior in irregular motion scenarios.

This article explores specific conditions within the partition realm where the standard additive representation holds. Specifically, we analyze situations where hook lengths can be expressed as the sum of two distinct units or three distinct units. Moreover, we seek to identify all possible combinations of parts that meet these conditions, in addition to understanding the distribution of hook lengths that meet these conditions within the partition realm.

In quantum mechanics, particle tunneling is evident in a variety of processes including electron transmission through potential barriers and fermion spin precession. In this paper, we establish a connection between these two phenomena by using the parameters from experimental studies of the Larmor clock to calculate the transmission time of electrons. Specifically, the experiment referenced is an electron beam scattering investigation against a thin copper foil carried out by the CERN LHC.

By employing the quantum field theoretical method to extract the dominant twist distributions from the mass spectra of mesons, P-wave meson states are analyzed. It's revealed that the maximal twist involved in the mass spectra of P-wave mesons is two. Certain function types, specifically $\delta_{k}(t)$ and $\delta_{kt}$, along with the Lindstrom-Meissner theorem-based function $\delta_{kt'}$, along with the function $\delta_{kt\neq kt'}$. These functions, previously unknown in the literature, have been utilized to derive the dominant twist distributions of P-wave mesons. Calculations based on the given functions have been conducted for the P-wave mesons, specifically $P$-waves, to determine their dominant twist distributions. The results of the calculations, derived from the dominant twist distributions, correlate well with the established spectral function $\phi_{P_{1}}_{\mu}^{(1)}(\omega;\mu)$ of $P$-wave mesons, obtained from perturbative QCD.

Using the Groenewold-van Dantzig theorem, we find the underlying phase space representation of a quantum nonlinear operator that creates and annihilates a Bogoliubov mode in a Bose-Einstein condensate. This representation involves overcomplete coherent states involving $\pi$ phase shifts. The obtained coherent operators are then applied to the study the nonlinear interactions of Bogoliubo v modes in a one-dimensional cavity containing two-level atoms. Using the coherent operators, we represent the Bogoliubov vacuum as a nonlinear function of the field operators of the one-dimensional cavity. In the context of one-dimensional Cavity Bose-Einstein Condensates, we examine the no-go theorem involving no no-go theorem involving squeezing of a quantum mode in a multi-particle system. This investigation also includes a comparison of three nonlinearly coherent operators that can represent the Bogoliubov vacuum. Although all three representations are equivalent, they exhibit distinct behaviors in the context of one-dimensional BEC in terms of Bogoliubov vacuums, squeezing, and entanglement.

This article extends soft principles to all field configurations and explores their implications for scattering amplitudes and symmetry algebras. Focusing on finite-energy sl(2|3,1) and u(2|3,1) algebras generated by the Poincaré generator and a new 'leg' generator, we reveal that their impact is inherent in the previously determined u(3,1|4) and u(2|3,1) BMS algebraic structure. Considering an experiment with an irregularly increasing, exponentially growing field, we show that higher-order soft terms derived from this are naturally incorporated within the BMS framework. Moreover, our results provide a clear connection between the new 'leg' generator and existing supertranslation charge. They also reveal that the impact of an irregularly increasing, exponentially growing field on subleading soft terms, derived from this, can be expressed through a generalisation of a 'hard' conservation law, and therefore these terms are naturally incorporated within the BMS framework.

The requirement for an online collective continual learning (OCCL) framework, which learns and adapts to a series of distributions without limitation, is becoming increasingly necessary for real-world scenarios. Current solutions, however, are typically confined to learning sequences with a predetermined number of distributions. To address this, we propose the creation of a neural framework for OCCL that can function without restrictions on the sequence length (number of distributions) and that learns and adapts (updates parameters and allocates new categories) as long online frames (time steps) unfold. To facilitate parameter and distribution adaptation, we develop a parameter adapter using a distribution's mean and covariance to normalize data, while a new category allocator based on the highest confidence and highest confidence difference with existing categories is introduced. To increase the effectiveness of the allocator in length-uncertain online sequences, we propose a sequential allocation strategy. To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed framework, two challenging length-uncertain scenarios are created: (a) the distributions in the learning sequence can be randomly divided into two groups, with the allocations taking effect immediately after the first group is encountered. (b) Similar to scenario (a), but the allocations take effect only after the second group is encountered. Experimental results show the proposed framework's high performance on two datasets, particularly in scenario (b). To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to address the length-uncertain OCCL problem from a neural framework perspective.

The concept of shapes has been further defined by considering the union of the point set X and its dual EX as a single entity. This revised definition is referred to as a generalized shape. Specifically, a generalized shape can be viewed as a closed subset of the subsetoid ${\langle}X,EX{\rangle}$ in the context of the Boolean algebra formed by the subsetoid's powerset. Furthermore, every generalized shape corresponds to an outer measure, which is defined as the subsetoid's measure relative to the subsetoid $EX$ in the context of the Boolean algebra. Moreover, every generalized shape with a finite corresponding outer measure of EX determines a metric d on X, such that the point set X is complete and the four-point set ${\langle}x,y,z,u{\rangle}$ is metrically indistinguishable if and only the corresponding metric distances d are equal. This is referred to as the Ricci flat four-point set ${\langle}x,y,z,u{\rangle}$.

In this study, we examine specific kinds of permutation functions defined over $\mathbb{F}_{q^{3}}$ that achieve a significant result - they create a one-to-one correspondence between $\mathbb{F}_{q^{3}}$ and $\mathbb{F}_{q^{3}}\times \mathbb{F}_{q^{3}}$. These specific kinds of permutation functions are called complete permutation functions and they have been fully characterised in this study under what conditions they exist. Moreover, various counting methods were also provided in this study to determine how many such functions of a given degree exist.

A major global concern, chronic intestinal parasitic infections rob people of strength and speed, impeding their ability to earn a living and achieve full potential.  In an effort to thwart the spread of these diseases, which claim the lives of over 21,000 people every day, experts turn to computer-aided techniques to classify the different species of these intestinal parasites.  By applying computer vision methods to examine slide samples, researchers have made significant headway in classifying ecto- and endoparasites under study.  Specifically, they have applied various approaches, including feature extraction and machine learning, to achieve impressive results.  In an effort to enhance accuracy, we recommend using the XGBoost library in conjunction with Belief Networks to analyze ecto- and endoparasites.  Our results indicate that Belief Networks outperform traditional machine learning approaches, showcasing exceptional potential in the study of intestinal parasites.  We have released our source code on GitHub, welcoming other researchers to build upon our work in this vital field.

To assess variability in parameter estimates, researchers examined a reinsurance arrangement involving an involved loss-sharing agreement between a power-varying ratio, an increased ratio, and an exponential increase in ratios. Assuming knowledge of model drift and a fixed variance, the prior distribution of model drift and the maximum likelihood estimate of variance are both explored as potential methods to estimate model parameters in this complex model. Notably, when the prior distribution of model drift is used, the corresponding maximum likelihood estimate of model drift can be directly derived from the resulting output. Simulation experiments revealed that model drift and jump-averaged mean performance, as well as variance, converged quickly in a large dataset. Furthermore, the convergence of bias was also observed to be relatively fast. This was further validated by applying the approach to a subset of real-world data.

This research presents a new approach to proportional-integral-derivative (PID) control by employing a reliable on-line algorithm to determine optimal gain settings for a linear system. Utilizing a stochastic dual simplex method with a genetic filter, the method can efficiently calculate optimal gain settings in conjunction with control input signals, such as those utilizing pulse distance modulation (PDM). Through this approach, the model can easily accommodate actuator failures in simulation. Additionally, the method is capable of identifying feasible control inputs to stabilize unstable systems. This technique has been successfully tested on a non-linear dynamic model of a rudder and a non-linear quadcopter model, ultimately resulting in the development of a novel pulse duration modulation (PDm) control strategy, dubbed PIDA-PDm. Further analysis compared the newly developed approach to established PID control methods, revealing that PIDA-PDm can stabilize an unstable system in both steady and fluid flight modes, stabilize a marginally stable system in fluid flight mode, and maintain stable performance in stable system in fluid flight mode with reduced vibration, comparable to the best conventional PID controller.

This article outlines the primary features of pion-nucleon interactions at low energy, 
as established through empirical research, and examines current high-energy experiments.

The Large Hadron Collider at CERN will be upgraded to the Comprehensive Large-scale Activity for Hard interaction particles Interaction point LHCb's foward cup system with an extension to explore new physics, expecially in the field of physics beyond Standard Model with both high precision and at a high rate. In preparation of this upgrade a technological upgrade is also taking place, involving a deep extension to the CMS tracker system, including an increase in luminosity to achieve similar physics results as in the past but with an extension in luminosity to explore new physics faster. The CMS pixel detector will also undergo technological upgrade with all components being customized for this purpose. In the course of this upgrade a total of 50 pixel blade prototypes were produced and tested in a beam with 25 GeV electrons, among these 10 were instrumented with added custom electrical signal tracing technology allowing for precise analysis. In this paper we will present the results from these 10 prototypes instrumented with the ability to trace the electrical signal, these results will be compared to the average predicted value and the origin of the background signal identified. Moreover these results will be published for the first time.

We have used a machine learning-based system to categorize 2,988 active galaxies hosted by galaxies with redshifts less than one, which were identified through the Subaru Hyper Suprime-Cam survey. By classifying these galaxies into bulge-dominate, disk-dominate, or transition types, we observed that the new machine learning method produced similar results as a machine learning method by Willner et al. (2018) but with a 30% improved classification accuracy. When we compared the new hosts to a control group of normal galaxies, we found an increased occurrence of bulge-dominate and transition galaxies while also a decreased occurrence of disk-dominate galaxies at higher masses. This implies a stronger preference for the host galaxies to have a bulge when they are more massive. Furthermore, we found that the hosts with bulge-dominate or transition galaxies have a higher amount of super massive black holes compared to those with disk-dominate galaxies, according to a previous study by Marques-Chapas-Méndez et al. (2017). This supports the idea that the growth of super massive black holes is associated with dense, massive galaxies which also contains a dense bulge.

High-energy density atomic nuclei are constructed through an intricate allocation of total phase-space resources. Specifically, total phase space is divided among the relative motion between particles and their internal spatial arrangements. In high-density nuclei, like those near the neutron drip line, a considerable portion of phase space is dedicated to minute interactions among particles right at the threshold of spatial overlap. Through an examination of Monte Carlo calculations involving a wide variety of even-even nuclei in the Hartree-Fock mean-field framework, it's been determined that, in even more densely packed nuclei like $^{16}$Ly and $^{10}$Li, a substantial fraction of phase space is indeed devoted to high-energy states influenced by short-range nuclear forces, particularly those related to the monopole and quadrupole operators. However, in more loosely structured nuclei like $^{11}$Li and $^{6}$He, the phase space allocations are vastly different and primarily dominated by the monopole component related to the monopole operator. These empirical observations are significant for the optimization of Monte Carlo calculations involving short-range nuclear forces and, more broadly, in the study of short-range properties in dense nuclei across the chart.

Recent breakthroughs in deep learning technology have led to successful applications in various fields, but its usage in complex-valued data is limited due to a lack of suitable learning approaches. The existing methods directly apply real-valued deep learning solutions, despite the unique characteristics of complex data such as its ability to represent phase information. A new type of deep learning architecture called Complex Convolutional Neural Networks (CCNNs) has emerged as a potential solution. However, CCNNs are still in their infancy and there is a shortage of effective training approaches. This paper aims to bridge this gap by proposing a novel form of co-domain equivalence called the 'rotative bias' that allows for the development of complex-valued neural networks from their real-valued counterparts. The proposed method is compared against existing approaches such as the 'ignoring phase' and 'treating as real' strategies, with results showing its superiority based on various performance metrics. The study utilizes a range of supervised learning applications, including two binary and two multi-class image classification problems, to validate the proposed approach. Overall, the rotative bias technique is shown to effectively capture phase information, resulting in significant improvements to accuracy, an increased range of expressible outputs, and a reduced impact on training time.

We examine the concepts of saturation and geometric scaling in QCD, initially focusing on the longitudinal momentum distribution of gluons within high-energy nuclei.  In this context, saturation occurs when gluon density is so great that it prevents further increase, which is mathematically represented by the gluon distribution per momentum, and leads to patterns of geometric scaling that can be observed at various scales.  Once the relationship between parton distribution functions and momenta is understood, this knowledge can be applied to understand the behavior of jets produced in high-energy nuclear collisions, where physical processes occur at very low and extremely high momentum ranges.

The prevalence of low-metallicity stars in the Milky Way raises significant concerns about the long-term viability of advanced lifeforms on exoplanets. Utilizing the Conjugate Gradient method to efficiently solve complex 2D gas dynamics and Euler equations, this study simulates the interaction between a star and a compact planet, factoring in the unique characteristics of low-metallicity stars. By adjusting the input parameters, this simulation replicates the outcomes from previous studies and reveals how variations in the planet's mass and initial orbit size affect the resulting distribution of mass on the star. Building on these findings, this study delves into the potential consequences of these interactions for planetary systems, with a particular focus on scenarios where one or more planets are within orbital proximity to the star.

The art of making predictions involves evaluating the performance of different forecasting methods, where classical statistics once reigned supreme, machine learning has revolutionized the field, providing a vast arsenal of powerful forecasting techniques. Our objective is to introduce a cutting-edge statistical toolset for assessing the reliability of machine learning forecasts. Leveraging the uniqueness of financial literacy as a field that is neither purely theoretical nor fully established, we showcase the application of this new toolset in predicting future financial behaviors based on past events and questions. Our analysis highlights the benefits of using this new toolset, demonstrating that the traditional measures of evaluating forecasting methods, such as the Dollar Metric and Washington Metric, have shortcomings, particularly in situations where the forecast distribution spans a wide range and the observed verification loss is sensitive to significant extremes. Consequently, we propose an alternative approach using a new metric for evaluating performance and sensitivity analysis. Our study reveals that the proposed method offers better results than the traditional measures and provides valuable insights into the capabilities and limitations of forecasting methods, ultimately helping users to accurately assess their performance and identify areas for improvement.

Quantum artificial intelligence systems hold great promise in addressing complex computational problems more efficiently than their classical counterparts. Among various quantum models, the Ising model has shown significant potential due to its versatility and range of applications. However, realizing large-scale quantum systems, essential for AI model development, is hindered by limitations of Landau-Zenner tunneling. To overcome this, researchers are exploring specialized topological superconducting qubit platforms that could facilitate the creation of large, interconnected qubits, such as those needed for self-organizing maps. Recent breakthroughs in this direction have been achieved, enabling the possibility of scaling up quantum computing systems, including the development of the quantum artificial intelligence system SQUID. This system is based on the Ising model and features non-stoquastic interaction Hamiltonians, providing an advantage in solving specific K-Satisfiability problems. Furthermore, its compatibility with the topological qubit platform makes it a promising candidate for scaling up. Furthermore, researchers have the potential to adapt the solution to the widely applied multi-layer perceptron model.

This paper explores a subset of nearly contact manifolds, denoted by $\mathcal{M}$, and a set of submanifolds, denoted by $\mathcal{S}$, where $\mathcal{S}$ is a subset of the tangent space at each point of $\mathcal{M}$. A specific type of submanifold, known as a distorted product pointwise semi-inclined submanifold, is also defined in this context. The paper will establish a specific relationship, denoted by $\lambda$, between $\mathcal{M}$ and $\mathcal{S}$, and show that, when specific conditions are met, $\lambda$ can be used to determine whether a certain subset of $\mathcal{M}$, denoted by $\mathcal{S}_\lambda$, is indeed a submanifold. The paper will also derive several key properties related to this type of submanifold, including its normal curvature, first local radius, and total mean curvature vector. The paper will also investigate the relationship between certain subsets of $\mathcal{M}$ and explore specific examples that demonstrate its findings.

The PALEOCCENE concept is proposed to achieve sensitive detection of nuclear recoil energy at keV levels without adding external parameters, by utilizing the interaction between 2D arrays of aluminum oxide color center nanocrystals and target nuclei. This is based on existing research demonstrating nanocrystals' responsiveness to beta decays at various energies. By arranging the nanocrystals in a gravitational field and recording changes in their optical properties over time, it is possible to calculate the distribution of recoil energies. Simulation results indicate that crystalline samples with high density and arranged in specific orientations can efficiently detect elastic neutron scattering from hydrogen at energies below keV. Furthermore, similar device architecture can be used to detect various other interactions, including ion scattering and some rare processes.

This study examines colloidal particles in a dynamic fluid, which is in contact with a solid surface with fluctuating activity. We focus on large particles and narrow peaks, and investigate how these particles move towards areas of highest activity. Using computer simulations, we calculated the velocity of the particles and found it directly proportional to a specific energy gradient. However, this velocity can be affected by the distance between the particles and the solid surface, especially when particles are close to reaching the solid surface. If the particles are very close, their movement towards the gradient is blocked and their movement towards the solid surface is slowed. To understand these behaviors, we developed a mathematical model that takes into account different types of energy, including interactions with the solid surface and the particles' own motion. This model helps to explain how these particles move dynamically in a complex environment.

This research examines the spectral density of two-dimensional multi-component Fermi liquids with scalar interactions, focusing on regions near certain critical points known as magnetorons. Unlike the theoretical frameworks provided by conformal field theory and bosonization, our computational approach based on density-matrix renormalization group allows us to explore broad spectral regions, including those influenced by charge density waves and superconductivity. We discovered multiple magnetorons within the $n=0$ SU($m$) sequence, characterized by spectral changes and signaled by growing dressed electron densities. Furthermore, within the $n=\pm 1$ SU($m$) sequence, we identified magnetorons modulated at wavevector $|\phi|$. Through constrained density-matrix renormalization group methods, we also tracked the evolution of spectral density within the $n=0$ SU($m$) sequence, revealing the total regulations of Fermi liquid spectral density at magnetoron critical points.

Infected individuals within a network spread their infection to a limited number of adjacent nodes. The rate at which they infect these neighboring nodes is denoted by the contact rate. Noting that the contact rate can be manipulated, a more detailed model considers each infected individual as representing a contact rate within a defined radius. Using Poisson distribution, an anchored Markov chain model is developed by representing the contact rates as the sum of two terms - mean and variance. Analyzing this model's transition rates reveals they are represented by eigenvalues of an explicitly defined matrix, whose diagonal elements are rooted in stochastic processes describing the disappearance and transition of infections. By applying a geometric approach, an expression is derived for these eigenvalues, allowing for the identification of dominant eigenvalues through stochastic process limit analysis. Consequently, critical fundamental parameters, such as how long a disease remains active, how many infected nodes there are at any given time, and the likelihood of an outbreak, are determined. Additionally, a classification system for network structures is thus established, leading to the discovery that open boundary networks and circular networks are particularly susceptible to certain types of infections.

We examine the method of defining the direction of the cosmic axis using the maximum probability map based on WMAP 3-year data, using the MCMC method to derive the confidence intervals for the orientation parameters. Our results are consistent with those using the maximum likelihood estimate, but our approach offers an advantage in avoiding the 'X' problem that can occur when trying to define the direction of the cosmic axis using the temperature distribution alone. In addition, we confirm that the cosmic axis is likely to be associated with the direction of the quasar z= 1111, previously identified by Nishizaki et al. (2003). Our results also show that the cosmic axis is likely to be associated with the anti-galactic pole, a finding that supports the Gappert-Gott hypothesis that the galactic plane is not unique in the universe.

Natural language can be used to specify tasks in goal-conditioned reinforcement learning, but agents often struggle to understand natural language objectives due to ambiguities and indirect meanings. Our study focuses on reference as a primary source of natural language-induced confusion in reinforcement learning settings. Two novel experiments using ABLATION, a robotic pushing platform, demonstrate that current algorithms, which are designed for natural language objectives, consistently falter on problems involving reference issues. Additionally, our analysis reveals that these algorithms' weaknesses stem from shortcomings in their ability to learn safe and efficient action sequences. Finally, we propose and evaluate different family of algorithms, called Goal Modifiers, which can directly address the reference ambiguity and significantly improve task completion rates and efficiency.

Quantum channel shadow tomography offers an effective approach to accurately determine the statistics of an unknown quantum channel that operates on density matrices, utilizing only classical resources and having a relatively low computational demand compared to other fully nonintrusive methods. This method has distinct advantages - it does not require direct access to the quantum channel and does not need to perform numerous quantum experiments; it only needs to calculate classical probabilities. The method outperforms other nonintrusive methods in terms of efficiency as it eliminates the need to directly measure the quantum channel, which may be difficult or even impossible to do, and does not involve the exponential increase in complexity associated with other methods. We present a new version of shadow tomography that focuses specifically on determining the statistics of quantum channels and shows that for certain channel statistics such as higher-order moments and characteristic functions, the required number of terms in the shadow operator can be significantly reduced - from $D^2$ to $\mathcal{O}(\log^2 D)$. The work also offers a new perspective on the applicability of the convex shadow tomography of matrices for determining mixed states, showing that it can be reduced to the case where it needs to determine the coefficients of only $2n$-degree orthogonal polynomials over the unit sphere $\mathbb{B}^{n-1}$ instead of the full $D$, where $D$ is the dimension of the Hilbert space, by utilizing the methods of classical approximation and Carleman's strong minimum principle

This research provides a comprehensive set of inequalities, known as the Keen inequalities, which pertain to shapes within two-dimensional space that exhibit convex properties. At its core, this problem seeks to establish precise bounds for a specific expression, R, in relation to the incorporated Cheeger constant, s. Key results derive algebraic equations where R is in relation to s, with one equation proving s can be represented as a function of R, and vice versa. Furthermore, this study introduces novel inequalities for combinations of s and R, with these new inequalities being a refinement of prior works by Keen. To support this, this research draws from previous studies involving Dirichlet and Neumann problems related to Laplace's equation, as well as properties inherent in uniform shapes.

This study investigates the most suitable flight path for a fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicle to complete a mission within a predetermined time frame. The objective is to determine the flight path that minimizes the energy required for the vehicle to carry a payload, subject to flight time and payload stability constraints. To achieve this, the vehicle's trajectory is broken down into continuous segments and its energy consumption is modeled using a simplified variable based approach. A mixed-integer non-linear programming strategy is employed to optimize the flight path. The proposed method can handle various payload shapes and its computational complexity is independent of flight time, making it more efficient than other approaches. The results show significant reductions in energy consumption, averaging between 50% and 75%, while also decreasing fuel consumption by up to 25%.

In multilayer graphene, fluctuations around a neutral Fermi liquid that exists in the system are analyzed through the renormalization group method. The coupling of charge and spin densities between layers is found to eventually become strongly coupled and highly unstable. This occurs regardless of the strength of coupling, and when couplings between layers are varied, the system exhibits multiple points where the Green's function becomes non-fluctuating. The results also indicate that increasing the number of layers enhances these instabilities, and the unconventional antiferromagnetic, QCD, and chiral spin liquid phases that exist in single-layer graphene are instead replaced with an unconventional dimer spin liquid and dimerized superconductor candidates.

Research into nanomaterials that survive under extreme conditions is rapidly gaining momentum. The confluence of theoretical and experimental advancements in materials synthesis and analysis at the nanoscale is key to achieving continuous control over the properties of bulk materials by regulating the characteristics of individual atoms or molecules. Thecurriculum development in materials science is becoming more dynamic due to the intersection of materials science and chemistry, accompanied by innovative teaching methods and tools. The resulting advancements in high-throughput nanomaterials synthesis, analysis, and assembly is transforming understanding and work at the nanoscale, with potential to deliver cutting-edge technologies in the near future.

Our investigation utilizes an ultra-stable Sc2TbN@C80 molecule on an epitaxial h-BN layer on Ni(111) and employs Scanning Tunnelling Microscopy combined with density functional theory to explore room temperature chemical stability, molecular motion and interactions on the substrate. The results reveal that Tb is favourably positioned in an octahedral environment. The Tb atom's spin is shown to influence charge distribution, leading to a slight contraction of the outermost Sc2N molecule. The Tb atom's magnetic properties also create a spin-polarized contrast in an STMs image of a Tb-free Sc2N molecule on the substrate. The presence of a Tb atom, however, results in the reversal of magnetic polarity.
