We have experimentally demonstrated and analytically demonstrated the mechanism of charge tunneling between a quantum dot and a superconducting island within a 2DEG material. The quantum dot's position within the material's potential landscape can be observed by utilizing its associated quantum fluctuations. This allows the dot to move back and forth between different energy states controlled by applying a precise voltage to a nearby gate. Our study has shown that when the quantum dot and the superconducting island are in close proximity to one another, they form a single entity that can be observed through measurements of current fluctuations. This combined entity can then be driven back and forth between different energy states by adjusting the gate voltage, and in doing so, we are able to identify all of the energy states involved in the system through both current fluctuations and power spectroscopy. This particular single-electron system can be characterized as being in the weak coupling regime and our study has shown that one of the key characteristics of this system is the flipping of Cooper pairs. This behavior is similar to but distinct from the shifting of single electrons between two energy states, and our study has shown that this particular phenomenon can be observed despite the presence of multiple energy states. The study has also revealed that localized single-electron tunneling events can influence measurements of current fluctuations even when the quantum dot and the superconducting island are in the weakly coupled regime. This particular effect can be reduced in magnitude but cannot be made extinct by increasing the coupling strength between the quantum dot

Recent research on hyperbolic systems of conservation laws with an entropy condition has highlighted the presence of discontinuities that are not necessarily self-similar in nature. These unusual spaces of such self-similar solutions have led to the development of a framework for defining suitable contractive conditions that apply to Kruzhkov's entropy condition, especially in the context of the inhomogeneous scalar conservation law. This has resulted in the establishment of Lp-Lipschitz bounds for solutions with such contractive properties, effectively generalizing recent findings by Kim and Shvydkov. Specifically, this study proves the existence of Lp-Lipschitz bounds for solutions within the space of entropic discontinuities, under the condition that p lies between 1 and infinity. Moreover, this research further expands upon previous work by Tavella in a variety of ways, including the extension of her results from scalar to system equations, the relaxation of requirements surrounding the spaces of self-similar solutions, the relaxation of assumptions surrounding potential singularities, and the demonstration of Lp-Lipschitz bounds across multiple variables.

This study presents an approach to generate perpetual views, achieved by combining a established inversion technique with a novel training method for the diffusion model. In the first stage, we use a confirmed rotation function and a iterative optimization process based on the OptAfN inverse lighting method, which enables the establishment of an initial eternal view representation for any given image under any rotation. Notably, our eternal view representation is independent of the actual rotation. Following this step, we train the diffusion model using the established eternal view representation, which results in a model capable of generating perpetual views. We evaluate our method using the NCL-TAIR dataset and the public datasets STARE2, DeepView2, and FlyingText, across various established metrics, finding that it outperforms existing eternally-view-producing models.

A novel, data-centric strategy is proposed to forecast, improve, and regulate chaotic and nonlinear processes within networks. This approach relies on dynamic long short term memory neural networks to create predictive models using real-time data, without the need for process-specific formulas or theories. To assess its effectiveness, this method was tested on modeling, predicting, and regulating epidemic outbreaks using the SIS model. This simulation showed that the model can predict outbreaks based solely on historical data, refine such predictions over time, and be regulated using control theory to prevent desired outcomes like vaccination targets, with promising prospects for extending this technique to other complex systems.

The Rayleigh-Plateau instability occurs when a liquid column is formed on a solid surface, specifically when a fiber is immersed in a liquid. The onset of this instability in such scenarios has significant bearing on how particles are dispersed during the production of fibers with embedded particles. Research has previously examined the dynamics of the Rayleigh-Plateau instability at the interface of a fiber and liquid, with a focus on how the viscosity of the fluid in question varies. Specifically, this has involved comparing the behavior of a fiber immersed in a liquid with a solid coating, effectively consisting of a series of particles at the liquid-fiber interface. Notably, this coating can be treated as having a effective viscosity. The present study builds on previous work by accounting for the actual distribution of particles at the liquid-fiber interface, instead of a solid coating, and, as such, this is referred to as the slip-augmented Rayleigh-Plateau instability. The effective viscosity resulting from this distribution is then used in the governing equations of the fiber and the Stokes equations for the liquid. The work involves both theoretical calculations and numerical simulations, the latter being performed using the finite element method, with a focus on the behavior of the liquid layer as the fiber is raised at a constant velocity. The results demonstrate the role of particle distribution in the onset of the instability, with a greater number of particles increasing the time to instability. Furthermore, this time can be affected by the velocity of the fiber and the size of the particles

The 1D Hunter-Saxton system, having connections to crystalline curvature flows and liquid crystals, guarantees the existence of solutions for any time interval. Researchers have proved that if the initial conditions and system parameters meet certain regularity criteria, the solution will also meet these conditions, plus an additional estimate related to the parameter's regularity. This solution's properties can be seen as a form of "Lipschitz sensitivity" regarding the system's parameters. This analysis builds upon a broader study of 2D Hamilton-Jacobi equations by Briani, Fraunfelder, and Sarac, applying the concept of "Lipschitz regularity" within the context of viscosity solutions.

Evaluating scoliosis using ultrasound imaging is an efficient and low-cost method with rapid results, but it has limitations with manual scanning techniques, including user variability and potential errors. As robotic scanning with ultrasound offers greater precision and objectivity, it could be a more reliable option for assessing scoliosis. This study compares the dependability of robotic ultrasound scanning with manual methods in detecting scoliosis in children. Scoliosis in 60 subjects was assessed using both robotic and manual ultrasound techniques, with scoliosis confirmed through radiography. While both robotic and manual scans showed high sensitivity (100% and 96.7%, respectively) in detecting scoliosis, the robotic scan exhibited greater reliability, with a coefficient variance ratio of 0.44 compared to the manual scan's 0.96. As a result, the robotic scan performed better in detecting scoliosis, with more reliable results.

This study proposes an anonymous approach to generating speech, allowing for creating various speech durations while preserving their inherent unity. A significant challenge in speech synthesis is maintaining continuity when synthesizing utterances of differing lengths. To address this, we developed a novel method using a non-statistical approach, leveraging a central point (median) to form the syntax and semantic structure. This structure, composed of a sequence of medians representing phonetic sounds, word types, and sentence patterns, serves as the framework for synthesis. A key aspect of this method is modeling the dependencies between consecutive central points to capture the natural correlations in speech. Furthermore, we identified specific central points to encode non-phonic sounds like breath, pauses, and fillers, and explored techniques to optimize the decoder to maintain consistency in durations during consecutive sentences. Ultimately, this approach can unify sentences of varying lengths within connected discourse.

Recent advancements in NLP have successfully applied deep learning models to various text-based classification tasks, including hate speech detection on microblogging platforms. Previous studies have measured the effectiveness of contextual information by comparing the performance of models using word and character-level encoders. This work presents an efficient model that combines the strengths of both approaches by integrating a character-based RNN for feature extraction, which outperformed the existing models on X-HATE and Twitter-Bot datasets, achieving an accuracy of 84.19% and 81.11%, respectively.

This research focuses on a multi-input multi-output (MIMO) communication framework in which sender and receiver are unaware of the transmission channel. To overcome this challenge, a method has been developed to encrypt messages in a manner that allows for efficient data recovery at the receiver, without necessitating any modifications to the existing protocol. By applying the concept of feature swapping, introduced by Gabor-Duniz et al. in 2021, this approach builds on the foundation laid by earlier work. Although the proposed method achieves some level of security, it suffers from certain shortcomings, as demonstrated in this study. Furthermore, an enhanced version of the scheme has been introduced, providing a secure comparison with the existing solutions.

This research surveys numerous datasets comprised of historical manuscript images, emphasizing the development of efficient image capture technologies, dissemination, and the pivotal role of computational methods in their analysis.

This study focuses on implementing a flatness-based robot controller for a
cranesheet assembly in an industrial robot setting, utilizing joint position and
force measurements. Given the unavailability of joint torque sensors, a novel
approach is presented that relies on deriving this torque via the robot's
inertia matrix, as identified by Simulink/Matlab. Despite offering a theoretically
valid solution, this method is impractical for real-world use due to computational
constraints and numerical issues associated with large robot models. Thus, a
digitally-efficient method for directly estimating torque via joint position and
velocity is proposed, along with an adapted torque estimator that integrates
these estimates with measurements from load sensors. The effectiveness of this
approach is supported by simulation and real-world testing, including evaluation
of the estimator's impact on controller performance using the critical fast
approach time constant as the sole performance metric.

A novel method is introduced to analyze extensive data on individuals' health over time, which is denoted as Multiple State Evaluation. This approach differs from traditional multistate models by accounting for various health outcomes simultaneously, taking into consideration their interrelated effects. It is exemplified using real-world data from a study on myocardial infarction patients, where multiple factors contributing to health over time are examined, including physical limitations, weight issues, blood pressure levels, cholesterol levels, smoking, and other factors related to recurring heart issues. By modeling these interdependent outcomes as fundamental components, their co-occurring effects can be interpreted in terms of predicted time spent in each state, rather than focusing solely on the occurrence of specific events. These interpretations can be utilized in two ways: by modeling the distribution of time spent in each state and those that follow, or by identifying the factors that maximize the likelihood of spending time in certain states, while minimizing the risk of spending time in others. With the ability to assess time spent in multiple states that may be of interest, this method offers a high level of flexibility in its applications. It is through the use of real-world data from patients with myocardial infarction that the authors of this paper, for the first time, showcase the capabilities of this novel approach, which can be utilized across a wide variety of research fields.

The electronic ground state of small molecules is modeled using a multigrid approach centered on Hartree-Fock theory, with computations divided between a strong scaling multikernel GPU algorithm for the orbital structure and a floating point quadrature method on the CPU to determine the orbital integrals in the Hartree-Fock minimization, thus enabling efficient computation on a wide range of molecules.

In a graph, the FDp parameter introduces a complexity threshold to the problem of computing a graph's metric dimension (GD). This involves identifying the smallest possible set of vertices that allows any other vertex to be uniquely determined by its connection to this set of nodes. The FDp parameter essentially measures the minimum required size of such a determining set when certain nodes are already accounted for. This framework enables the GD problem to be treated as the FDp parameter with p set to 1. The FDp parameter can be closely linked to key structural graph attributes like minimum feedback vertex number n(FV), maximum clique order k, and tree-width t. This study seeks to establish upper bounds for FDp in graphs with certain attributes, like those containing a fixed tree, which has a limited number of its own (h < p). It also looks into scenarios where the determined tree has its roots in an attribute-free subgraph (p < h). The research further explores how these findings can be applied to the GD problem, yielding an algorithm that can solve GD on graphs with the attribute-defined property. The FDp parameter can also be analogously applied to the problem of computing strong metric dimension, which is known to be equivalent to the GD problem in a specific formulation.

A new class of directed area parameters for two-dimensional vector fields defined within bounded domains in mathematical space is introduced and investigated. These parameters yield scalar field values that represent the interaction between local velocity and directional properties, which can be used to determine the directed area properties of subdomains separately. Necessary and sufficient conditions for the directed area parameters to be non-zero or negative are established, and for any given parameter value, the necessary and optional range is identified. A method for calculating directed area parameters relies on minimizing the difference between the desired parameter value and the corresponding values of subdomains, and is referred to as the power framework of directed areas. The power framework is applicable not only to continuous but also to discrete vector fields, and it is shown to consist of a convex optimization problem whose solution is unique. By utilizing the power framework, anisotropic diffusion equations with directed properties can be formulated, which select between the properties of subdomains separately and the overall field. These equations are able to preserve the directed properties of specific subdomains while smoothing others, and they are shown to consistent with the directed area parameters. Additionally, it is demonstrated that minimizing the difference between the desired parameter value and the corresponding values of discrete sub-domains in discrete vector fields leads to directed area properties consistent with continuous vector fields.

To analyze the behavior of intense rainstorms in highly climate-changing atmospheric conditions, we examined Euler's equation in a limited series expansion. Our findings show that these storms take the form of solitary nonlinear waves. Specifically, we found that large-scale rainstorms in areas with high temperatures and high altitude regions are characterized by strong and sudden episodes of heavy rainfall. Additionally, our research provides a mathematical explanation for the periodic fluctuations in rainfall patterns observed in such environments.

New twistor constructions have been developed for Yang-Mills fields with increased spin and for self-dual Yang-Mills fields with increased spin. Although both cases demonstrate similar pattern behaviour, they differ fundamentally. The pattern in the Yang-Mills fields with increased spin is represented by a higher-form gauge connection, whereas in the self-dual Yang-Mills fields with increased spin, it is represented by a zero-form gauge connection.

The use of noisy labels in machine learning can hinder the accurate prediction of disease states in medical imaging. To tackle this issue, traditional image processing techniques that rely on median polishing come up short, especially when dealing with significant levels of noise. To bridge this gap, a novel restoration method called BLR is introduced, combining the benefits of both median polishing and soft-label correction to effectively eliminate noisy labels. Built on a Bayesian framework, BLR offers a systematic approach to finding the optimal configuration for performing restoration tasks. Through practical evaluation, BLR has demonstrated its capability to accurately remove noisy labels and achieve high noise tolerance, with impressive results seen in the form of improved overall accuracy and robust performance in the presence of noise, as evidenced by our experiments on multiple datasets.

Consider a function $f$ belonging to the Sobolev space $W_{p}^{(s)}(\Omega)$, where $s\in\mathbb{N}_0$, $\Omega$ is a bounded domain in $\mathbb{R}^n$, and $f$ restricts to $W_{p}^{(s)}(\partial\Omega)$. Let $\Delta_\Omega$ denote the Laplace-Beltrami operator over $\Omega$. A recent paper (Arado, 2021) provided an integral estimate for the $L_q(\Omega)$-norm of an interpolation operator when combining functions $f|_{\Delta_\Omega(\Omega)}$ and $f|_{\partial\Omega}$. This current discussion presents an improved estimate that surpasses the previously known outcome.

A random walk with a related movement restricted to a defined neighborhood has been explored, along with its transition likelihood matrix. This study focuses on deriving a distinct polynomial form for the transition matrix, which is tied to a random walk's basic characteristics, including its probability of returning to the starting point and overall connectivity in a graph. This research reveals how the features of a random walk are reflected in the transition matrix. Additionally, two applications of this research have been proposed, including an analysis of the influence of a graph's degree distribution on its polynomial form and a classification method for pairwise coherence in graphs based on the required properties for coherence.

In this work, we establish a fundamental understanding of time and its function within the logical framework of HOL, building upon the fundamental logic principles.  Time is identified as advancing in a consistent and uniform manner.  Initially, we establish the concept of a point in time, represented as a real number.  Subsequently, we define a function that links times to their descriptions, characterized as the passage of a unit of time.  Additionally, we define a family of sets that encompasses all possible scenarios in which the passage of time is happening simultaneously.  This fundamental understanding of time is then utilized to define the concept of a timed system, represented as a subset of the combination of times and the system's original definition, already established within the fundamental logic principles.  This timed system's state dynamically changes over time.  This work is an extension of the earlier research conducted by Rushby on the dynamic description of a system's state, building upon his findings to define the concept of a timed system, rather than rushing into the broader realm of temporal logic.

A novel approach has been developed that uses the analysis of data from turbulent flows to improve upon an existing model for simulating the impact of turbulent waves at the boundary of a surface. Specifically, this new approach is applied to the $\mathcal{P}$-model, which is part of a larger predictive framework known as the coherent bed topography framework. By leveraging a sophisticated method for translating data, known as WiSE-PCR, the new results reveal a more precise correlation between measured turbulent wave patterns and the characteristics of the underlying surface topography. Furthermore, the new results suggest a more accurate representation of the average characteristics of turbulent waves, including their speed and persistence times. Importantly, this new approach is versatile and can be applied to a wide range of turbulent flows, including those that are wave-driven and those influenced by wind or currents.

This study demonstrates the presence of self-dual (topological) solitons in a newly formed model by combining the Skyrme model with the Born-Infeld infant theory of electromagnetism. The infant model incorporates electromagnetism in a non-linear manner similar to the Bogomol'nyi-Prasad-Sommerfield model, yet differs through its non-trivial vacuum expectation value for the field strength. The incorporation of this infant electromagnetism into the Skyrme model yields self-dual equations reminiscent of those from the Bogomol'nyi-Prasad-Sommerfield model, but with an additional non-linearity that varies with temperature. Although an analysis of the model's thermodynamic properties is beyond the scope of this study, it has been shown that the inclusion of non-linear infant electromagnetism in the Skyrme model yields self-dual equations.

By incorporating a random potential with a quantum of flux, researchers examine the interplay between disorder and magnetic field in creating Weyl semimetal topological transitions. Within a specific flux-density range, this model reveals that disorder can trigger PT symmetry breaking even in the absence of a magnetic field. The existence of PT broken states is confirmed through analysis of the Green's function and the self-energy, with each corresponding to distinct, stable solutions. The solutions include PT broken Weyl semimetals and PT broken Mott semimetals, with the latter characterized by vanishing quasiparticle densities of states at the Fermi level. The proposed theory also suggests that degenrate bands can transform into two-band Weyl bands through disorder, with the quasiparticle excitation at the Fermi level exhibiting delocalization. The findings of this investigation can be extended to study PT symmetry breaking in two-dimensional and three-dimensional systems with applied Berry curvature. The proposed model provides a foundation for exploring topological phase transitions, quasi-Hall effects, and anomaly flows in systems with combined effects of disorder and magnetic field.

A novel UAS-NP (unidirectional asymmetric split-nanoptode) structure is introduced, combining both plasmonic and photonic mechanisms to achieve a unique optical phenomenon, referred to as the "unidirectional luminous light source". This name accurately represents the robust, single-mode, highly-unidirectional, high-efficiency and robust light emission provided by UAS-NP. UAS-NP's design enables the efficient excitation and emission of localized plasmons through a simple design, further enhanced by its intrinsic asymmetry and a specific structural dimension, resulting in the highly directable and efficient emission of light. Additionally, the design's inherent asymmetry and specific geometry also enable the realization of various polarization properties. Furthermore, the tight light confinement and high local enhancement factors generated near the UAS-NP's aperture facilitate enhanced emission, while maintaining a relatively small and practical size for integration with nanodevices. These combined features make UAS-NP an optimal choice for the implementation of nanophotonic applications and nanodevices.

A novel theory of anomalous shielding has been proposed for granular media, stating that external stresses are fully or partially blocked through unique internal stress configurations. Although supported by prior experiments, these studies had limitations, applying only to specific scenarios of two-dimensional stress configurations. This research addressed this limitation by testing anomalous shielding in three-dimensional cavities filled with granular material to determine if the effect could be generalized. To validate this hypothesis, numerical simulations were performed to measure pressure around a 3D cavity when subjected to an external stress, and compared with data collected from a balanced 3D setup, both featuring a central puncture and identical granular material. While the results showed anomalous shielding occurring in the balanced system, numerical simulations indicated that the effect was not applicable to two-dimensional stress configurations, and thus did not contradict existing knowledge. Furthermore, it was observed that the subject's geometry and whether the stress was applied from within or externally affected the occurrence and intensity of anomalous shielding. These findings support the idea that anomalous shielding has hidden instances of partial shielding within three-dimensional stress configurations.

Our research results for silicene embedded with Mn on a boron nitride surface are obtained through density functional theory. Silicene, a single layer of silicon, exhibits hexagonal symmetry similar to germanene, with its band gap being exceptionally low at 0.8 eV. When combined with a 2D boron nitride substrate, the addition of Mn adorns significantly alters the electronic properties of silicene. Remarkably, the manganese-adjacent phosphorus sites transform into a quantum anomalous Hall state featuring a nearly perfect 100-meV full energy gap at the Dirac point. Moreover, the presence of a substantial magnetic moment of 3.0 microbengtens per manganese atom is consistent with earlier studies, as well as the spin-polarized properties of silicene-Mn-phosphorus-silicene-Mn (M-P-M-P) systems. Consequently, the quasiparticle spectra of this system manifest differing energies in response to spin orientation, thereby classifying this system as a quasiparticle-based device yielding anomalous resistance with respect to magnetic fields applied in a perpendicular direction. Furthermore, the breakdown of valley symmetries, as witnessed through the allocation of spin, sublattice, and orbital characters, results in the shifting of Mn d-orbital based bands both above and within the gaps of silicene. The origin of the ~100 solar mass black hole located at the center of the galaxy's Sgr A East remains a mystery, despite multiple theories. Recent studies of the galaxy's X-ray emission suggest that the blast from a stellar explosion occurred approximately 300-400 years ago. Our analysis relies on a semiempirical method used to calculate the three-dimensional distance between our sun and Sgr A East within the galaxy, taking into account the variations in the galaxy's stellar population and motion. Building upon previous estimates by others, we arrive at a different conclusion regarding the timing and energy release of the stellar explosion in Sgr A East. Our analysis also considers the implications of the explosion's onset on nearby gas and stars within the galaxy, particularly with respect to the 16 Cygni A star which is believed to be moving towards the galaxy's central black hole.

In multi-category text classification, common oversampling methods, such as random oversampling and the border oversampling method, are often used to tackle the class imbalance issue. These methods are typically applied to the original data set. A new oversampling technique known as artificial minor class oversampling was proposed in a 2017 study and provides better performance than traditional methods. This paper builds on that research by introducing two more artificial oversampling methods: artificial oversampling based on distribution and artificial oversampling using topic features. These new techniques not only address the class imbalance but also incorporate distribution characteristics and topic features. Experimental results using 14 data sets show that the proposed methods outperform the existing border oversampling method. Analysis of the performance gains reveals that the proposed methods are particularly beneficial for datasets with either significant class imbalance or a large difference in class sizes.

This study examines how COVID-related coverage in the United States varies across regions, including those with high-risk infections and higher mortality rates, more extensive reporting by local news sources, and varying relationships between national and local news coverage. Utilizing data on COVID fatalities, regional characteristics, and news coverage from COVID resource websites and databases (such as COVIDTrack), and news coverage from databases (such as NewsData, Dataverse, and MEDUSA!), the researchers analyze correlations among coverage, infections, and fatalities. Key regions, including the South and Midwest of the U.S., are identified with distinct patterns of COVID coverage. Notably, areas with higher COVID risks tend to receive more local and less national news coverage. These findings have significant implications for digital COVID resource websites, especially those targeting specific regions or news audiences. 

Using data from April 2020 - December 2020 (pre-vaccination period), the analysis reveals that local news coverage is more strongly associated with COVID infections than national coverage, whereas national coverage is more strongly associated with COVID fatalities than local coverage. 

The results also illustrate the differing regional characteristics of COVID coverage, with areas having higher coverage rates (e.g., the Northeast) exhibiting a negative correlation between national and local news coverage, whereas those having lower coverage rates (e.g., the South and Midwest) exhibit a positive correlation. 

Ultimately, the study's findings offer valuable insights into understanding COVID coverage in the U.S., including its regional disparities and variations in national and local news

The Rapid Multipole Method, used to compute interbody interactions in N-body problems, is generally conservative with physical properties, such as position, velocity, and angular momentum. Despite its conservation properties for position and velocity, the conservation of angular momentum depends on the specific implementation of the method. Older versions of the code failed to conserve angular momentum but recent updates, specifically introducing conservative handling of angular momentum, ensure the method also conserves angular momentum calculations.

Despite the proton's inherent polarization, the outgoing electron and proton created in $e \vec {p} \to e \vec {p}$ are not guaranteed to be polarized due to a lack of net orbital angular momentum transfer between them. To investigate this phenomenon, we calculate the conveyance of polarization conveyance for this specific process and compare it to analogous models. Our study indicates that the conveyance of polarization in $e \vec {p} \to e \vec {p}$ is zero at leading order in QCD but can be nonzero at next-to-leading order. This result is relevant in understanding how high-energy protons lose their polarization when scattered through the Bjorken-$x$ range where Drell-Yan and Weizs\"acker-Williams processes dominate the photon distribution function $\gamma^{0} (x,Q^2)$, and an analogous conclusion can be drawn for their antiparticle counterparts.

To improve training methods for non-parametric models, we developed an algorithm that generates synthetic data by incorporating results from parametric models. This technique, called PEMD, enhances the training set with artificial examples, produced either directly or through a series of transformations, using inputs and corresponding outputs from a parametric model. This generated data exhibits characteristics similar to those in the original set, as evaluated by both visual and statistical methods. Importantly, PEMD produces data that can be successfully inverted, meaning the outputs can be accurately reversed to retrieve the original inputs. Experiments conducted on a mix of artificial and real data across various tasks demonstrate PEMD's efficacy, with successful application of Invertible Volume Factorization and both high accuracy and efficiency achieved in comparison to models trained solely on real data. This paper explores PEMD's theoretical underpinnings and showcases its practical utility.

Measurements of cross-section ratios involve producing a Higgs boson pair in association with a W or Z boson, compared to single Higgs boson production with the same vector boson. These ratios, calculated using data from 2015-2018 in the 13 TeV proton-proton collision experiment at the Large Hadron Collider, are performed with the ATLAS detector at the European Organization for Nuclear Research. Each channel is categorized by the vector boson, with the resulting cross-section ratios calculated for both the charged W boson and the charged neutral Z boson, referenced against the Standard Model. Due to the similarities in the signal and background profiles between the channels, the ratios are highly insensitive to acceptance and kinematic factors, and are found to be in alignment with the predicted values from the Standard Model at a magnitude of 0.2 with a corresponding uncertainty of 0.06.

The study of quantum systems, particularly complex quantum phenomena such as entanglement and non-locality, has been hindered by the lack of suitable quantum instruments. By combining cutting-edge technology with innovative digital signal processing techniques, it's now possible to develop sophisticated quantum systems that were previously inaccessible. This work showcases a cutting-edge digital implementation of an alkaline spin maser, capable of generating gigahertz microwave light, which sets a new standard for solid-state masers in terms of coherence and efficiency. The system's performance serves as a benchmark for current quantum measurement technologies. Additionally, the study of this system's properties is complicated by the presence of technical noise, an issue that can be overcome using novel quantum correlation measurement techniques. The system's performance serves as a benchmark for current quantum measurement technologies, and further optimization is predicted to bring the system close to the quantum limit, with significant potential for improving sensitivity in precision measurements and quantum information applications.

We've compiled a comprehensive database of K3 varieties within the moduli spaces of K3 surfaces, accounting for all variations arising from tropical alterations, factorizations, projections, concretizations and Weil restriction processes. Besides, our collection also includes K3 varieties associated with Shimura varieties of dimension three. This list is structured in terms of the K3 genus, referencing Dolgachev's classification to the extent it's already documented, while incorporating some insights from [DO17]. Furthermore, this database offers precise descriptions of K3 varieties, coupled with explicit formulas for their Picard numbers, dimensions of identity components, the numbers of factors in their rational Picard group and the dimensions of associated Siegel domains.

A certain neutralino model with a specific mass range that isn't too high is particularly appealing because it doesn't have a maximum mass limit that would clash with the universe's large-scale structure observations. This model stands out due to its connection to a deteriorating neutralino where the mass and life expectancy are directly linked, with the life expectancy being determined by the universal expansion. This relationship means the neutralino isn't affected by the universe's large-scale structure observations, with its mass range being confined to less than 4 TeV. This neutralino is likely to be detected in experiments such as the HL-LHC and future colliders like the SPPC, through production coupled with neutral bosons. Furthermore, studies of the neutralino's life expectancy are linked to its life expectancy gamma radiation spectrum, with its total emission following a power law. This emission is concentrated in gamma rays with energies in the MeV range, which can be detected by space-based observatories like the IMAGINE mission.

A graph embedded in a surface with a certain radius of curvature is referred to as a "thick graph." The genus of such a graph can be determined using the z-eigenvalue counting function. Given a closed surface of a certain radius of curvature and an integer pair (p,q), we can construct a sequence of z-eigenvalues for its p/q rotational graph. This paper provides a method to approximate the genus of a thick graph with boundary from a approximation of a particular function related to its z-eigenvalues. The method also identifies criteria for when this function is an algebraic counting function. This article builds upon prior research, including studies by the authors on thick graphs and surfaces with spherical curvature, and by other authors on hyperbolic graphs.

This research presents a communication-efficient algorithm for solving large-scale distributed convex optimization problems. By leveraging inexact gradient computations in the randomized Newton method, we reduce communication costs at both the gradient and Hessian collection levels. We provide comprehensive analysis of the algorithm's convergence and optimal iteration efficiency. Through simulation experiments, we evaluate the performance of our method against alternative solutions in the distributed optimization domain.

This study focuses on the recognition of hate speech within social media content, 
devoting particular attention to Urdu and Hindi content sourced from Twitter. 
Given that social media platforms have restricted user content, this research 
delivers an essential exploration into the application of machine learning for 
hate speech detection, as well as the use of sequence-to-sequence models for 
offending statement rewording. The investigation employs neural network models 
such as CNN, LSTM, and 3D-CNN with attention, as well as the Turku Neural 
Corpus for labeling data; associated results reveal that LSTM delivers the 
highest accuracy when re-stating offends text, achieving 74.5% accuracy on the 
test set. Additionally, this research employs the Social Media-HateSpeech dataset 
for training and testing purposes, also including a new dataset generated from 
Bengali language posts, labeled by humans as offends and not offends, utilizing 
a 10-fold cross validation method; results show that LSTM with 3D-CNN and Deep 
Corel RNN deliver 67.0%, 64.0%, and 62.0% accuracy, respectively. The study 
also demonstrates that LSTM with 3D-CNN and Deep Corel RNN with 3D-CNN and

A key component for accurately locating nuclear events in high-resolution gas time projection chambers will be a detector that effectively tracks the movement of ions following a collision. Scientists have suggested several concepts for such a detector, including a "sensitive volume" defined by the electric field in the chamber, a movable gas volume over a stable substrate, and a rotating plane that splits the chamber into two sections. In this study, the potential of these designs as freely movable detectors have been evaluated to determine their effectiveness in detecting the movement of ions using both analytical models and simulations. Our analysis shows that all the concepts have drawbacks, however, and can be challenging to maintain a consistent electric field in moving parts, and it may be difficult to achieve the desired level of gas purity in free-moving gas volumes. In contrast, a rotating detector appears to be feasible but may have limitations in terms of speed and the number of events it can detect. Overall, a detector based on a freely movable gas volume may be the most viable option but will require significant advancements in terms of design and technology before it can be effectively implemented.

In many situations, such as when evaluating commercial drivers, it is necessary to combine the capabilities of machine learning models with human expertise. Typically, decisions are made by combining the outputs of these models, but this can lead to undesirable outcomes, particularly in contexts where certain actions may have undesirable social implications, such as discrimination. To address this challenge, we have developed a novel method of incorporating human oversight into decision-making processes. Our approach, which involves having an expert review specific details from the scenario and potentially override the initial decision, is more efficient and effective than previous methods, which require constant involvement from an expert. We have found that this method receives higher ratings of fairness and is as effective in making accurate decisions as using machine models alone.

We report on the findings of the Out-of-Lexicon (OOL) Challenge from the 2021
Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP), featuring
two parallel challenges: OOL Encompassing Domain Jumps and OOL in Contact Languages.
The OOL Challenge aimed to tackle the issue of out-of-lexicon words in text
processing, specifically in the context of part-of-speech (POS) and lemmatization.
Given an English text, participants were asked to predict the POS and base form
for each word given a pre-trained language model. This model was based on the
XLM-R, which was trained on 100 languages, including nine indigenous languages
of North America, and was subsequently fine-tuned on the CoNLL-2009 Test Data.
The task drew a significant number of participants, with 219 submissions from 74
teams across both challenges. To recapitulate the challenges' results, we present an
overview of the winning approaches, describing how they leveraged the
multilingual XLM-R model for POS and base form predictions in the given English
text. We detail our team's solutions to the two challenges, focusing on how we
leveraged the model for POS and base form predictions that incorporated both
known and unknown words. Notably, we discovered that the unknown word that fell
outside the standard English lexicon tended to be a word from the indigenous
